FIELD TRAINING PROGRAM
Revised: August 23, 2024

Law enforcement, as a profession of public service, includes an ever-widening variety of tasks and responsibilities. The responsibilities of a patrol officer are extensive and may have far-reaching ramifications. In addition to good judgment and common sense, the officer must have knowledge of the law, Division training, and Departmental Policies and Procedures to effectively perform these duties. The Field Training Officer (FTO) teaches the Probationary Officer (PO) to apply knowledge gained at the Training Academy and enhances that knowledge by providing on the job training and instruction. The Field Training Program will provide quality training, and fair and impartial evaluation of every PO assigned to the program. The Field Training Program consists of 15 weeks of training which is divided into four (4) phases. By the conclusion of the Field Training Program, a PO must demonstrate knowledge and proficiency in daily basic patrol functions.
Mission Statement

The Columbus Division of Police, in keeping with community expectations for professional police service, has established the Field Training Officer (FTO) Program. The mission of the Columbus Division of Police FTO Program is to prepare POs to perform the essential duties of a police officer and to enhance the professionalism of the Division of Police through continuous quality improvement.
Goal

The goal of the Field Training Program is to develop a police officer capable of performing at an acceptable level as a one-officer patrol unit in a safe, efficient, reasonable and professional manner.
DEFINITIONS
(These definitions are written specifically related to the Field Training of Columbus Police Officers)

Acceptable - A performance rating system category used to evaluate a PO’s performance on the Daily and Weekly Performance Summaries. This rating category is used when PO performs a specific job function, completes a patrol task and/or paperwork in a timely manner and without FTO assistance or direction.
Active Status – An FTO’s ability to be assigned a PO for training. To retain active FTO status, an FTO must be available for two phases of training for every eight phases.
Activity Summary - Located on the bottom of the Weekly and Daily Summary. This section is used to maintain a tally of the more common tasks of a patrol officer.

Chain of Command – During Field Training, the FTO Sergeant shall be included in the FTO’s and PO’s chain of command where appropriate. The FTO Sergeant shall be apprised of any problematic performance or concerns involving the FTO or PO.

Checklist FTO forms- Forms which provide a basic outline to address training, Policies and Procedures, patrol tasks and officer safety issues that the PO may be expected to perform during dispatched or self-initiated runs. FTOs will use a checklist form to evaluate the PO’s performance on each run. Forms may also be used as a review or debriefing form. Each completed checklist form should be included with the Daily Performance Summary packet.

Corrective Training - Training conducted by any member of the Division of Police that addresses the PO’s performance deficiencies. All corrective training by anyone other than the assigned FTO or immediate supervisor, must be approved by the assigned FTO, FTO Coordinators, or FTO Sergeant. All corrective training shall be documented on approved FTO forms.
Daily Performance Packet - A packet that consists of a Daily Performance Summary, FTO checklist forms and copies of any additional reports/paperwork that FTO chooses to attach.

Daily Performance Summary - Division form U-10.174. Form completed for each tour of duty during each Phase. The form lists all performance categories, rating systems, and activity summary. FTO will use the rating system to evaluate the PO’s daily performance for each category, except on Limbo Days.

Executive Training Board (ETB) – The Executive Training Board is the ultimate, collective, decision-making authority of the Field Training Program. The ETB is comprised of the Special Services Assistant Chief, the Operations Branch Assistant Chief, The Support Branch Assistant Chief, the Public Accountability Deputy Chief, and the Patrol Deputy Chief.

Field Training Board (FTB) - The FTB consists of the six (6) Patrol Commanders, the Training Bureau Commander, the Training Bureau Lieutenant, FTO Sergeant, and FTO Coordinators (2). The FTB gives final approval or disapproval of FTO Applicants, and approves training curriculum.

Field Training Committee - A committee comprised of six (6) elected senior FTOs from each of the six Patrol Zones, FTO Coordinators (2), and FTO Sergeant. Members will recommend and implement changes within the program as needed.

Field Training Guide - The guide is issued to each PO by the FTO Sergeant/Coordinators and it includes the Training Summary, Lesson Plans, Location/Orientation Guide and copies of FTO paperwork and forms. The guide will be forwarded to the FTO Office at the conclusion of field training.
Field Training Office Coordinators (2) - Police Officers assigned to the FTO Office in a full-time capacity.

Field Training Officer (FTO) - Any officer that completes the required annual training a determined by the Field Training Board and is in active status as determined by the Field Training Program standards.

Field Training Office - Located at the James G. Jackson Columbus Police Training Academy, 1000 N. Hague Ave. Columbus Ohio, in the Basic Training Unit. The office is staffed by the Field Training Sergeant, 2 Field Training Coordinators, and any FTOs temporarily assigned to the Field Training Office.
Field Training Office Sergeant - The Sergeant assigned to the FTO Office in a full-time capacity.

Limbo Day/Period - A set amount of day(s) at the beginning of each training phase in which the PO is not rated. The period is designed to assist the PO in becoming acclimated to the new environment, the FTO and the daily tasks associated with functioning as a one officer patrol unit.
Location Guide - Located in Field Training Guide. Used to record the date of orientation for specific locations.

Not Observed (NO) - A performance rating system category used to evaluate the PO’s performance on the Daily and Weekly Performance Summaries. This rating category is used when the PO did not have the opportunity to perform a specific job function or patrol task.

Not Responding to Training (NRT) - A performance rating system category used in evaluating a PO’s performance on the Daily and Weekly Performance Summaries. This rating category is used when PO has displayed a pattern of documented poor/deficient performance in a specific job function, patrol task, and/or paperwork - despite receiving corrective re-training to address the performance. PO does not accurately complete paperwork and continuously is unable to complete paperwork and tasks in a timely manner. Use of “NRT” is used in conjunction with an “Unacceptable” rating and must be supported by documentation listed in the corrective training/ retraining section.

Performance Category - Any one of the thirty (30) categories that make up the Standard Evaluation Guidelines. Each category relates to a specific job function determined to be pertinent in order to function as a one-officer Patrol Unit.

Performance Rating - The rating system used to evaluate the PO’s performance for each Performance Category. Consists of five ratings to include Acceptable (A), Responding to Training (RT), Unacceptable (UA), Not Responding to Training (NRT) or Not Observed (NO).
Phase - A set period of weeks in which the PO is assigned an FTO and evaluated daily (excluding Limbo Days) on his/her performance.

Phase Goals - A predetermined number of patrol tasks to be completed during each phase. The Phase goals are guidelines to promote exposure, proficiency and ensure consistency in the training of basic patrol tasks.
PO Strengths - A section located on the Weekly Performance Log. Used when the PO has displayed consistent acceptable ratings in any of the Performance Categories in any given week of training.

PO Weaknesses - A section located on the Weekly Performance Log. Used when the FTO has documented deficient or poor performance by the PO and PO requires direction and assistance to complete the patrol task.
Probationary Officer (PO) - Any officer that has not completed his/her one-year probationary period.
Probationary Training Sergeant – The sergeant assigned to the Probationary Unit full time.
Probationary Training Officer (2) – Field Training Officers assigned to the Probationary Training Unit in a full time capacity.
Probationary Period - The amount of time that the Probationary Officer is on probation as defined by Civil Service Rule, currently 365 days from date of graduation.

Recommendation - FTO’s opinion as to whether the PO is released or terminated from field training program. Typically, made at the conclusion of the PO’s 15th week of training; however, a recommendation to terminate training may occur during any training phase and requires immediate notification and involvement of the FTO Sergeant.

Responding to Training - A performance rating system category used to evaluate a PO’s performance on the Daily and Weekly Performance Summaries. This rating category is used when PO reasonably performs a specific job function, completes a patrol task and/or paperwork, but requires minimal FTO direction/assistance. The task may or may not be performed within a timely manner.
Senior FTO - An FTO is considered “senior” after completing four (4) coaching phases as the assigned FTO. Generally, senior FTOs will be used for Phase IV training.
Senior Patrol Commander - Chairperson for the Field Training Board. Determined by the period of time a commander has in grade.

Standard Evaluation Guidelines (SEGs) - Measured standards within all of the thirty Performance Categories that are used to rate a PO’s performance. The SEGs were developed and established to ensure standardized consistent evaluation for all POs. SEGs reflect Division Rules, Policies, Training, Basic Patrol Tasks and Laws.

Summary of Patrol Activity - Located in the Field Training Guide. This document is used to enter the date when a particular topic is thoroughly discussed or demonstrated. FTO & PO are responsible for daily completion of Training Summary.

Suspension - An FTO’s participation in the Field Training Program may be temporarily suspended at the Direction of the Training Bureau Commander based on recommendations from the Field Training Sergeant and concurrence from the Basic Training Lieutenant.

Unacceptable - A performance rating system category used to evaluate a PO’s performance on the Daily and Weekly Performance Summaries. This rating category is used when PO displays poor/deficient performance in a specific job function, patrol task and/or paperwork and requires frequent FTO direction/assistance. PO does not perform task and/or paperwork in a timely manner.

Weekly Comment/Signature Form - Included in the Weekly Evaluation Packet. The document will include the comments and signatures of the PO, FTO, and FTO Office. The document is reflective of the PO’s weekly performance, and acknowledges review of the packet. At the conclusion of Week 15, the FTO will recommend whether the PO is released from field training or terminated from the Division of Police.

Weekly Evaluation Summary/Packet - It represents a complete summary of the PO’s performance for the week. The packet contains a Weekly Performance Summary, Weekly Performance Log, Daily Performance Summary for each day, Weekly Comment/Signature Form, completed checklist forms, and any additional supplements or copies of paperwork.

Weekly Performance Summary - Division form U-10.174 - Displays the total number of performance ratings the PO received for each performance category for the week. Also provides a weekly total in the Activity Summary area.
ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE
Executive Training Board
The Executive Training Board (ETB) consists of the following personnel:
The Special Services Branch Assistant Chief
The Operations Branch Assistant Chief
The Support Branch Assistant Chief
The Public Accountability Deputy Chief
The Patrol Deputy Chief

The ETB will serves as the ultimate collective decision making authority. The Public Accountability Deputy Chief will act as the Chairperson for the ETB. The ETB will convene to determine the retention of current FTOs when notified by the Training Bureau Commander of the suspension of an FTO from the program. The ETB will make a final determination on the status of the suspended FTO, to include: reinstatement to the program, suspension from the program, or permanent removal from the program.
Field Training Board
The Field Training Board (FTB) consists of the following personnel:
Patrol Zone 1 Commander
Patrol Zone 2 Commander
Patrol Zone 3 Commander
Patrol Zone 4 Commander
Patrol Zone 5 Commander
Patrol Zone 6 Commander
Training Bureau Commander
Basic Training Bureau Lieutenant (Advisor)
Field Training Office Sergeant (advisory capacity)
FTO Coordinators (advisory capacity)

The Senior Commander will act as Chairperson for the FTB. The FTB shall ensure that all Senior FTOs serving on the Field Training Committee are released from regular patrol duties when requested by the FTO Sergeant. The FTB will give final approval or disapproval for all FTO applicants, training curriculum, and any issue brought before them by the Basic Training Bureau Commander on behalf of the FTO Sergeant.
Field Training Committee
The Field Training Committee (FTC) consists of the following personnel:
Senior FTO from Zone 1
Senior FTO from Zone 2
Senior FTO from Zone 3
Senior FTO from Zone 4
Senior FTO from Zone 5
Senior FTO from Zone 6
FTO Sergeant
FTO Coordinators

The FTO Committee is designed to allow FTOs to become involved in the program to foster ownership and to reinforce professionalism and program integrity. The Zone Senior FTO is determined by a majority vote from FTOs assigned to that respective Patrol Zone. The Zone Senior FTO will be rotated on a yearly basis. The year may be extended by the FTO Sergeant in order to maintain continuity. Rotation will ensure that all eligible FTOs have an opportunity to participate and serve on the FTO Committee. The FTO Committee’s duties and responsibilities will include:

 Reviewing the FTO Manual, Standard Evaluation Guidelines (SEGs), FTO Guide, and FTO paperwork prior to the graduation of a recruit class to ensure that all material is current, within Division Policy, and reflects any changes in the law or procedure within the FTO Program
 Offer input on many aspects of the FTO Program
 Responsible for processing, interviewing and voting on new FTO applicants
 Provide detailed information and recommendations on applicants to the FTB to assist them in the completion of the selection process
 Must be willing to adjust his/her hours/days off to complete assigned tasks as needed
 Complete any additional tasks as assigned by the FTO Sergeant
Basic Training Bureau Lieutenant Advisor
The assigned Lieutenant’s duties will include:
 Serve as a liaison between the FTB and the Field Training Office Sergeant
 Serve as member of the FTB in an advisory capacity
 Oversee coordination of FTO program with Patrol Commanders
 Oversee implementation of proposed changes within the FTO program and office
 Ensure that the Field Training Office Sergeant is completing assigned duties
 Report FTO Committee recommendations to the FTB.
 Oversee FTO Committee operations and coordinate members’ release time with Patrol Commanders
 Complete FTO Sergeant’s yearly performance evaluation
 Oversee activities when a Probationary Officer is relieved of duty and ensure the notifications are made

Field Training Office Sergeant
The FTO Sergeant is responsible for overseeing all aspects of the FTO program. The FTO Sergeant’s duties and responsibilities will include:
Serve as member of the FTB in an advisory capacity
Have multi-shift responsibilities
Assigned to the Recruit Training Bureau under the appointed Basic Training Lieutenant’s Chain of Command
Will maintain and staff an operational FTO office at the Columbus Police Academy
Review weekly FTO packets to ensure that program guidelines are being followed and goals met
Monitor Weekly Packets and training phases for problems or negative patterns
Coordination of the FTO selection process and training of new FTOs
Coordination of annual in-service training for current FTOs
Coordination of trainings for patrol supervisors as needed
Introduction of FTO program to the current Recruit class
Coordinate phase assignments of Probationary Officers and Field Training Officers
Disseminate and Review annual FTO evaluations
Approve additional overtime for Field Training Officers as needed
Relieve Probationary Officers from duty as needed
Responsible for assembling the documentation for formal Recommendations of Termination to the Director of Public Safety
Relieve Field Training Officers from FTO duties as needed
Make recommendations regarding removal of an FTO from the program to the Training Bureau Commander
Convene, guide, and direct the Field Training Committee as needed
Coordinate record retention of all FTO packets according to Division Policy and applicable laws
Ensure that the Field Training Office Coordinators are completing assigned duties
Report to the Basic Training Bureau Lieutenant, FTB, and ETB as needed

Has the authority to recommend temporary suspension of any FTO from the program and will conduct an investigation, if necessary, involving the suspension. Any administrative investigation involving the suspension of a current FTO will be forwarded through the Basic Training Lieutenant to the Training Bureau Commander to determine if the FTO will be suspended from the FTO Program and make notification to the Public Accountability Subdivision Deputy Chief.
Ride with FTOs yearly to stay familiar with Patrol duties and responsibilities
Other duties as assigned by the Basic Training Bureau Lieutenant and/or the FTB
Field Training Office Coordinators (4)
The FTO Office is staffed full-time with two (4) Police Officer FTO Coordinators. The FTO Coordinators’ duties and responsibilities will include:
 Serve as members of the FTB in an advisory capacity
 Review weekly FTO packets to ensure program guidelines are being followed and goals are being met
 Complete tasks as assigned by the Field Training Office Sergeant
Ride with FTOs yearly to stay familiar with Patrol duties and responsibilities
 Report to the Field Training Office Sergeant and FTB as needed
Help with the Community Immersion program
The FTO office is also staffed with two full time FTO’s. The FTO’s duties are the same as the FTO Coordinators’ duties.
Field Training Officer

The FTO is an integral part of the Columbus Division of Police. The FTO is entrusted with the responsibility of developing and training the future officers of the Columbus Division of Police. The FTO’s duties and responsibilities will include:
Embrace the Field Training Program’s Mission Statement and Goal
Be thoroughly familiar with and obey all applicable laws, ordinances, Division Rules, Policies, Directives, and training that pertain to his/her employment
Ensure that each PO is given the opportunity to develop skills, abilities, and knowledge required to become proficient in basic patrol functions
Teach, train, and evaluate the PO on a daily basis in a fair, consistent, and professional manner
Document the PO’s performance on a daily basis in a fair, consistent, and professional manner
Recognize the PO’s and FTO’s responsibility to the citizens of Columbus and the Division of Police
Strive to create a positive training environment encouraging the PO to succeed and develop into a competent and professional police officer
Adhere to, and stress the importance of The Core Values of the Division of Police during the field training phases

Determine whether a PO meets the goals of the Field Training Program and is capable of performing at an acceptable level as a one-officer patrol unit in a safe, efficient, reasonable and professional manner

The applicant must complete an application supplied by the FTO Sergeant or FTO Coordinators. The application is to include a letter to the Chief of Police addressing supplied questions. The application is to be completed and returned to the Field Training Office.

text: Applications will be accepted during an open enrollment period following an announcement in the Daily Bulletin and/or Division-wide email. The following steps must be completed prior to the applicant being considered for the Field Training Program:
Field Training Officer Application
Supervisor Review
Peer Reviews (4)
FTO Applicant General Knowledge Test
EBU Sick Mark-Off Review
IAB/Discipline Review
Written Work Sample Review
Oral Interview
Supervisor/Peer Review

A Supervisor/Peer Review Questionnaire will be sent to the applicant’s immediate supervisor, two peers provided by the applicant, and two peers provided by the applicant’s immediate supervisor. The questionnaires are to be completed and returned to the Field Training Office.
FTO Applicant General Knowledge Test

The applicant will complete a basic knowledge test. The test consists of fifty questions that cover material found in Division issued inspectional material. The FTO Committee formulates the test with oversight by the Field Training Sergeant. If an applicant misses more than ten questions, he/she will be provided a second opportunity to complete a similar test. The Field Training Sergeant will determine when the second test is administered. If the applicant does not pass second test, he/she will be removed from the application process.

Applicants may appeal any answer marked as incorrect. Applicants must document concerns in writing, and cite the Division Resource where the correct or conflicting answer is located. The FTO Committee will review appeals and advise the applicant of the finding. If the appeals process determines a test questions to be erroneous or incorrect then it will be removed from all completed tests.
Applicant’s Work History Review

FTO Committee members will obtain a copy of the applicant’s EBU Sick mark offs, IAB Employee Report, assignment history, and written work samples (e.g., PremierOne Reports, packets, any other official document completed by the applicant that relates to duties of a patrol officer). The FTO Committee reviews this information for issues such as sick leave abuse or disciplinary actions. The FTO Committee also reviews the applicant’s thoroughness in documentation generated in the discharge of his/her daily duties.
Oral Interview

The applicant will participate in an oral interview conducted by the Field Training Sergeant and two additional FTO Committee members. Applicant will respond to a set of standardized questions, and discuss or explain any information or concerns identified during the applicant’s application process. A follow-up interview with the FTO Sergeant may be required to clarify or address any questions raised by the FTO Committee.

The FTO Committee will convene to review and discuss each applicant’s packet. The FTO Committee will vote to decide whether the applicant will be recommended for the program. A majority vote of the FTO committee will determine the recommendation. The FTO committee’s recommendation of each applicant will be forwarded to the FTO Board for final approval. The FTO Board’s decision is final and no appeals will be accepted.

Applicants that are accepted will be notified by the FTO Sergeant or Coordinators of his/her acceptance, and dates and times of all future training that is required. Applicants that are not accepted will be notified by the FTO Sergeant. The FTO Sergeant will supply the applicant with the reason(s) his/her application was disapproved. The FTO Sergeant may also suggest applicable training or work related experience that would assist the applicant to address any or all deficiencies as determined by the FTO Committee. Applicants that are disapproved are encouraged to reapply at a later date, provided that they meet all FTO minimum application standards.
FTO Mandatory Training

Upon acceptance into the Field Training Program, the officer will be required to complete the 40 hour FTO Orientation Course. The material covered in the training course will be approved by the Field Training Board. Upon successful completion of the course the officer will be considered a Field Training Officer and will be permitted to wear the FTO insignia pin on the right pocket flap of his/her uniform shirt.

Field Training Officers will also attend a minimum of 8 hours of In-Service Training annually. The In-Service training will be scheduled by the FTO Sergeant and approved by the FTO Board. Failure to attend the mandatory annual training will result in the FTO being suspended from the FTO program until the training has been completed. FTOs are encouraged to attend any additional training that would be of further benefit to them as an FTO. Preference will be given to active FTOs when applying for advanced training opportunities.

Evaluation of FTOs

In an effort to maintain a high standard within the Field Training Program, FTOs will be evaluated on a regular basis. The use of evaluations will allow the FTO to be critiqued in order to identify areas of strengths and weaknesses. The reviews will also be used to provide feedback in areas where the FTO may improve subsequent performance.

At the end of a PO’s field training phases, the PO is asked to complete an evaluation for each of the four FTOs that trained the PO. The evaluations do not become part of the FTO’s Division Personnel Employee File. The evaluations will be retained by the FTO office. They are reviewed to ensure the FTO Program is achieving its goals. The FTOs are permitted and encouraged to view the critiques. The evaluations are saved electronically in the PO’s file, located on the I Drive.

FTOs will also be evaluated annually by his/her immediate supervisor. The FTO Office will forward the evaluation to the FTO’s precinct sergeant, who will complete the form. The immediate supervisor will permit the FTO to review, make comments, and sign the evaluation. The patrol sergeant will then forward the evaluation to the patrol lieutenant for review and comment. The evaluation will only be forwarded to the patrol commander upon request or in the event of an unsatisfactory review. All completed evaluations will be forwarded back to the FTO Office. The FTO Sergeant and FTO Committee members will review any unsatisfactory evaluation. The FTO Sergeant will forward the recommendations of the FTO Committee to the FTB. The FTB will decide whether the FTO is retained by the Field Training Program.

section: Temporary Suspension or Removal from the FTO Program
text: If at any time an FTO fails to adhere to the established Minimum Standards, Policies, Procedures, and/or Guidelines of the Field Training Program, the FTO Sergeant may recommend a temporary suspension of FTO privileges. The reasons for suspension may be due to issued discipline, Chain-of-Command recommendations, and/or performance as an FTO. The FTO Sergeant will forward an explanation for the suspension and a recommendation regarding retention to the Training Bureau Commander. The Training Bureau Commander will determine if the FTO is suspended. If the Training Bureau Commander suspends an FTO from the FTO program, he/she shall notify the Public Accountability Deputy Chief of his/her decision so the ETB may convene and determine the final outcome. If the ETB’s decision results in further suspension or removal from the FTO program, the FTO may appeal his/her removal in writing directly to the Public Accountability Deputy Chief of Police. The Public Accountability Deputy Chief will then submit the appeal letter to the Chief for a final decision.
Resignation

Any FTO wishing to resign in good standing may forward a formal letter or a mail of his/her resignation to the FTO Office. If an FTO resigns in good standing, the FTO may reapply to the program, subject to current FTO application standards and criteria.

Additionally, any FTO leaving the program due to promotion should forward a formal letter of resignation to allow the FTO Office to ensure the list of available FTOs is current. This also assists the FTO Office in maintaining adequate staffing levels for FTOs.

section: The Role of the Field Training Officer
text: The Field Training Officer is the essential means by which the program’s goals are achieved. In addition to being a patrol officer, the FTO assumes responsibilities as a trainer and evaluator. As a trainer, the FTO must be knowledgeable in the many aspects of law enforcement, and be able to communicate that knowledge to the PO. The FTO must be motivated to involve the PO in a variety of experiences. The FTO is a good communicator who debriefs and discusses the PO’s performance with the PO in an open and objective manner in order to foster the PO’s development.

section: The Role of the Field Training Officer
text: Additionally, the FTO must be a skilled and consistent evaluator and documentarian. FTO is required to complete accurate and comprehensive documentation on a daily/weekly basis. This documentation serves to provide appropriate feedback to the PO and the Chain of Command. It is necessary for the FTO to be familiar with all of the Standard Evaluation Guidelines (SEGs) in order to provide consistent and fair evaluation. The SEGs are the established standard and rating system used by the FTO to measure the PO’s performance. Accurate and fair documentation is essential to the evaluation of the PO’s performance. FTO evaluations are used to determine if the PO meets the FTO Program’s standards. It is important to realize that a rating, especially “Unacceptable” or “Not Responding to Training”, is only a reference with little value if not supported by appropriate documentation. The FTO shall complete all required FTO documentation on a daily and weekly basis.

section: The Role of the Unit Sergeant
text: When POs are assigned to the Field Training Program, the duties of the Patrol supervisor become more complex. In addition to Patrol responsibilities, the precinct sergeant must ensure the training and evaluation process is accomplished. Various sources of information can be used to achieve these goals. Completed progress reports, verbal communications with the FTO/PO, and the sergeant’s personal observations of performance should serve as indicators of the PO’s development.

section: The Role of the Unit Sergeant
text: The sergeant and FTO must accept the importance of documentation during PO’s training. Documentation identifies both proficient and deficient performance and provides useful information to develop a plan for corrective action. It also provides a reference to respond to questions concerning the program and/or a PO’s performance. Particular attention should be given to written reports submitted by a PO to assess his/her ability to communicate important information. The sergeant must monitor the overall training and evaluation of the PO to ensure accuracy and objectivity. Each supervisor must offer assistance and advice to the FTO, and when appropriate, support and counseling to the PO.

section: The Role of the Unit Sergeant
text: Should a supervisor become aware of behavior or actions by an FTO that are detrimental to a PO’s progress, or the training program in general, the sergeant should attempt to correct the behavior, as well as bring the issue to the attention of the FTO Sergeant. If the problem is of such a nature that immediate action is necessary, the Unit Sergeant may immediately remove the PO from his/her assignment and temporarily place them with an alternate FTO. The FTO Sergeant will then reassign the PO to a new FTO in an effort to ensure that a positive training environment exists.

section: The Role of the Unit Sergeant
text: Throughout the field training process, the unit sergeant must be familiar with the progress of any PO under his/her supervision. A truly effective Patrol supervisor will work with the FTO to accomplish the goals of the training program. The sergeant should not undermine the training format used by the FTO. The FTO, being the most aware of a particular PO’s needs and abilities, should make the final determination as to training procedures.
Policies and Procedures
The following Policies and Procedures were developed to maintain the consistency of the FTO Program within the Patrol Bureaus.

1. The Patrol Commanders of the Division of Police recognize the importance of exposing Probationary Officers to as many different types of incidents as possible. Because of this, FTOs are given the authority to cross precinct/zone boundaries for the sake of training and exposure to crime scenes and unusual occurrences. The FTO must notify the precinct or covering sergeant when leaving assigned precinct/zone.

2. To retain active FTO status, an FTO must be available for two phases of training for every eight phases. Whoever violates this policy will be removed from the Field Training Program unless just cause is shown (e.g., illness/injury, temp non-patrol assignment, military deployment etc.).

3. FTOs will not be allowed to request a specific PO to train during any phase. FTOs will not generally be permitted to train POs known to the FTO prior to employment by the Columbus Division of Police in either a personal or professional capacity. The FTO Sergeant will work closely with the Training Academy Staff and all FTOs to place Probationary Officers in assignments that will benefit the training needs of the Probationary Officer.

4. FTOs should commit to coaching the entire phase when they are assigned a Probationary Officer. Taking time off during a training phase should be extremely limited. This is in order to maintain continuity in the training process. In the event the FTO will be unable to work a tour of duty, it shall be the FTO’s responsibility to find an alternate FTO for the Probationary Officer. The FTO can contact the FTO office for assistance in locating an alternate FTO. A Probationary Officer should not be placed with a non-FTO officer unless there are no trained FTOs available. The non-FTO officer assigned a Probationary Officer will not complete FTO paperwork or attempt to evaluate a PO’s performance.
5. Phase training of a Probationary Officer is challenging physically and mentally. Typically, back-to-back phases will be an exception and will only be done with permission from the FTO Sergeant.

6. Generally, only senior FTOs will be able to coach during Phase IV. An FTO is considered senior after serving as an assigned FTO for four (4) previous phases. The Phase IV FTO will make a final recommendation after Week 15 to release the PO from training or to terminate the PO from the Division of Police. However, an FTO may recommend termination during any training phase if the FTO has provided consistent documentation that the Probationary Officer does not meet the Field Training Program’s standards and goals.

7. The FTO Program recognizes the importance to document and communicate a Probationary Officer’s strengths and weaknesses as they progress through the training phases. This communication is used to identify performance areas which need additional training and exposure. It will be the responsibility of the FTO Sergeant/Coordinators to discuss and obtain such information from the current phase FTO and relay the information to the next phase FTO. In regards to the PO, the assigned FTOs are encouraged to communicate information pertinent and beneficial to the PO’s training and performance progress in a professional manner. This communication should be completed in a timely manner to ensure consistent training especially in identified areas of weakness. FTOs will be able to review all Weekly Performance Evaluations and any training records upon request. FTOs are encouraged to seek guidance from the FTO Office and Senior FTOs for assistance when additional training options are needed to address PO performance deficiencies.

8. The FTO Program has established Phase Goals which are a predetermined number of patrol tasks completed during a specific training phase. The Phase Goals are to be a guideline to promote exposure, proficiency and ensure consistency in the training of basic patrol tasks. FTOs are expected to train using the Phase Goals as building blocks to improve on subsequent performances.

9. The FTO and PO will review Unacceptable Performance Ratings from the previous tour by the beginning of the next shift. FTO will make the PO aware of consistent Unacceptable or NRT ratings in any Performance Category as soon as practical. FTO and PO will discuss the concerns and devise a training plan to address the weakness. The FTO shall immediately contact the FTO Office if the PO receives an “NRT” rating in any performance category. This will give the FTO Sergeant/Coordinators immediate feedback regarding PO’s weaknesses as well as corrective training/retraining of each PO during field training.

10. The FTO will be required to complete and assemble Weekly Evaluation Summaries and Packets. POs will be required to review the packet and complete the Weekly Comment/Signature Form. FTOs will electronically place a copy of the Weekly Summary to the appropriate folder in the FTO Drive (I:) and notify the FTO Office that the summary is ready for conversion. The packet should be forwarded within 3 days after the conclusion of the week. The FTO Office will convert the summary to a portfolio. When conditions exists that warrant review by the Probationary Officer’s Patrol Chain of Command, the FTO Sergeant will forward the package.

11. The FTO shall immediately contact the FTO office if he/she encounters personal or professional issues which will interfere with performing the duties and tasks of a training officer. FTO Office will reassign a PO if it is determined that the PO’s training is being negatively impacted.

12. The FTO will conduct a debriefing with the PO following traumatic incidents, including crime scenes that involve serious physical harm or death, traffic accidents (including PO involved), and any stressful event. If a PO participates in a debriefing session conducted by another unit, such as SWAT, the FTO will not be required to conduct a debriefing unless it is deemed necessary. Follow-ups will be conducted as needed.

13. The FTO will be provided 1 hour of overtime for each 8 hour shift they are assigned a PO, or 1.25 for each 10 hour shift. If the assigned FTO is not available, the PO will be placed with an alternate FTO. The alternate FTO will complete the Daily Performance Summary and forward it to the primary FTO. The alternate FTO will receive the 1 hour/ 1.25 hours of overtime pay for the shift that he/she trained the PO in lieu of the primary FTO. A non-FTO will not receive FTO overtime pay and will not document/rate the PO’s performance.

14. Upon completion of Phase I, Phase II or Phase III, the FTO will receive twelve (12) hours of vacation time from the City. Upon completion of Phase IV, the FTO will receive eight (8) hours of vacation time from the City. Payroll will not apply earned vacation time until the conclusion of the 15th week of FTO training. Vacation time cannot be used until it has been placed into the FTO’s time bank. For Phase I, Phase II, or Phase III, an FTO who works a five day, eight hour work week must perform the FTO role for at least 17 of the 20 day phase training. An FTO who works a four day, ten hour work week must perform the FTO role for at least 13 of the 16 day phase training. During Phase IV, an FTO who works a five day, eight hour work week must perform the FTO role for at least 14 of the 15 day phase. An FTO who works a four day, ten hour work week must perform the FTO role for at least 11 of the 12 day phase. This incentive has been agreed upon by the City and FOP.

15. The FTO may take the probationary officer to one (1) FTO subpoenaed court appearance during the PO’s 15 weeks of training. This is to occur only one time during the 15 weeks of training and the FTO/PO will log the attendance in the Field Training Guide. The FTO will explain all involved court procedures as they apply to the Patrol Officer at that time. The FTO will not take the probationary officer to court on the second day off unless the probationary officer has been subpoenaed to appear.

16. An FTO will be awarded an FTO Insignia upon successful completion of the 40 hour FTO Orientation Class. Upon resignation, removal from FTO status and/or transfer or promotion, the FTO will return the FTO insignia to the FTO Coordinators, unless the FTO has completed ten (10) phases of training. Upon completion of a 10th Probationary Officer training phase, the FTO will keep the FTO Insignia to display on his/her uniform.

17. Any active FTO is authorized to purchase at his/her own expense, the FTO patch to be worn on an outer garment. The approved outer garments are the light weight jacket and the heavy weight jacket. The FTO patch shall be placed underneath the Division patch on both arms. Upon resignation, removal from FTO status, and/or transfer or promotion, the FTO will have the FTO patch removed from outer garments.

18. Upon completion of four (4) Probationary Officer training phases, FTOs will receive the FTO ribbon to wear on his/her uniform. A star will be awarded for every additional four (4) Probationary Officer training phases. A maximum of four (4) stars will be displayed on the ribbon.

19. During Week 15 of Phase IV training, the FTO may wear plain clothes. The FTO will dress in accordance with the Division’s non-uniform dress code as stated under Directive 11.01 - Professional Appearance. The FTO will only use plain clothes training if the probationary officer has Acceptable performance ratings in all Performance Categories listed under Officer Safety, Judgment/Decision Making, and Self-Initiated Activity. The FTO will indicate the wearing of plain clothes on the Daily Performance Summary and Daily Log for that tour of duty.

20. Division computers assigned to the FTO Program will be issued by the FTO Sergeant to the PO for use by the FTO. FTOs using an assigned a computer shall comply with Directive 10.01. FTOs shall not download any software/programs, access any Internet sites deemed inappropriate and/or access any streaming audio or video. FTOs do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy when using a Division-Issued computers. Email and other computerized records are monitored and can be retrieved for administrative purposes. The PO shall retain control of the computer and take it with them to the following phase. All issued equipment will be returned to the FTO office at the conclusion of each phase.

21. The PO in an FTO unit shall log into the Cruiser Video System (CVS) at the beginning of the shift, entering the usernames for PO and FTO, Area/Zone, Shift, and Unit Number. PO shall ensure the CVS is operational, or advise a supervisor if the unit is not functional. Refer to Directive 11.02 - Cruiser Video System.

22. The PO and FTO shall both employ their issued Body Worn Camera (BWC) systems, ensuring the cameras are operational. PO shall report malfunctioning BWCs to a Division Supervisor. Refer to Directive 11.07 – Body Worn Cameras.

23. When marking in for service, the FTO/PO will advise radio if they will be working as a one or two officer FTO unit. During each training phase, it will be the assigned FTO’s responsibility to determine when the PO is prepared to mark in service as a two officer FTO unit.
Training Schedule

The Probationary Officer will complete a fifteen (15) week Field Training Program, which will be divided into four training phases. Each training phase will offer a new FTO and assignment to the PO. The purpose of a varied training schedule is to expose the PO to different FTOs, duty hours, patrol zones, and precincts. Each phase will incorporate a limbo period, during which the PO will be trained with no evaluations being conducted.

The FTO Program has established minimum standards or goals for each phase of training. These guidelines have been implemented to assist the FTO and PO by establishing a natural progression of training, with respect to common patrol tasks and paperwork. A structured program and schedule will offer the consistency necessary to support the FTO Program goal.
 Phase I: Phase I is four weeks in length. The limbo period for Phase I is the first Week of this Phase. Phase I will focus on basic patrol tasks such as report writing and traffic enforcement.

 Phase II: Phase II is four weeks in length. The limbo period for Phase II is the first two days of this Phase. Phase II will focus on report writing, traffic enforcement, conflict control and arrest situations.

 Phase III: Phase III is four weeks in length. The limbo period for Phase III is the first day of this Phase. Phase III will focus on conflict-control, self-initiated activity and reports and paperwork that accompanies such patrol tasks.

 Phase IV: Phase IV is three weeks in length. The limbo period for Phase IV is the first day of this Phase. Phase IV will encourage the PO to become more independent in regards to all patrol related tasks. At conclusion of 15th week, the FTO is required to make the recommendation to release the PO from training or to terminate the PO from the Division of Police.
FTO Probationary Period Phase

If the PO is recommended for release from the FTO Phase training, the PO will complete the FTO Probationary Period, which will extend 365 days from his/her graduation date. During this week, POs will be assigned to the FTO Sergeant/FTO Coordinators, where the POs will receive additional training related to his/her field training experience and any other classes the FTO Office deems necessary. The FTO Sergeant/FTO Coordinators will address administrative issues and provide POs with their Probationary General Relief Assignments during this week. The Probationary Officer will be assigned to the precinct sergeant, who will evaluate and document the PO’s performance throughout the FTO Probationary Period Phase.
Phase Specific Goals

The FTO Program has implemented Phase Specific Goals. Phase Specific Goals are meant to be achieved in order to improve proficiency and to ensure progression in the training of basic patrol tasks. FTOs are expected to train using the phase goals as building blocks to improve upon the PO’s subsequent performance. The Phase Specific Goals are guidelines to develop the Probationary Officer’s knowledge, skills, and abilities. The goals are designed to assist the PO in becoming more confident when responding to calls for service, engaging in self-initiated activity, and handling more complex patrol tasks over a period of time.

Documentation must be provided by FTO in the final Weekly Summary/Packet explaining why Phase Specific Goals were not met during any phase training. If an FTO is consistently unable to meet Phase Specific Goals, then the FTO’s completed Weekly Performance Summaries will be reviewed by the FTO Committee. Phase Specific Goals are as follows:

Evaluations

The FTO’s daily/weekly documentation in conjunction with Standard Evaluation Guidelines (SEGs) will be essential in determining if the PO’s performance meets the FTO Program’s goals and the Division standards. In order to accomplish a consistent and fair standard of evaluation, thirty (30) performance categories and five (5) rating systems will be used by the FTO to evaluate a PO’s progress and performance. The Performance Categories have been determined to be essential elements needed to function as a one-officer patrol unit capable of performing in a safe, efficient, reasonable, and professional manner. The categories were established after analyzing Division Rules, Policies, Directives, applicable laws, accepted police procedures, and training. FTOs must realize that rating system designations, especially “Unacceptable” or “Not Responding to Training”, are only references with little value if not supported by appropriate documentation. The FTO will be required to measure the PO’s daily performance against the SEGs unless the tour is part of the limbo period or the PO is assigned a non-FTO for the tour.
Limbo Period

The limbo period is designed to assist the PO in becoming acclimated to a new environment, the FTO, and the daily tasks associated with a one-officer patrol unit. The limbo period is a set amount of day(s) at the beginning of each phase of training during which the FTO will document dispatched, self-initiated, or training incidents on the appropriate FTO forms. However, the PO will not be evaluated. No evaluations will be made or recorded on the Daily Performance Summary during the limbo period. The FTO should initiate and demonstrate all police activity, provide training and instruction, and offer a review of procedures used by the Patrol Officer to the Probationary Officer. If applicable, the FTO should focus on the PO’s areas of weakness during the limbo period in an attempt to provide additional training. This will benefit the PO by providing additional exposure and instruction in identified areas of weakness.

Standard Evaluation Guidelines (SEGs)

The SEGs define thirty (30) performance categories and five (5) rating systems which the FTO will apply when evaluating a PO’s progress and performance. The performance categories are numbered on both the Daily and Weekly Performance Summaries. The performance category numbers will be referenced when the FTO completes the Weekly Performance Log - Probationary Officer “Strengths”, “Weaknesses”, and “Weekly Corrective Training” sections. It is important to remember that a PO’s performance must be evaluated against the SEGs and not personal perception. It is through the use of these guidelines that FTOs achieve performance rating consistency.

The FTO Coordinators and FTO Sergeant shall be notified when a PO receives an “NRT” rating. The FTO, PO, FTO Coordinators, FTO Sergeant and precinct sergeant will work together in an attempt to overcome the area of deficiency. An “NRT” rating is always used in conjunction with an “Unacceptable” rating.)

Duty Readiness
1. Report/Prepared for Duty

Appearance/Equipment – Evaluates ability to arrive for work in a prompt and timely fashion and in a neat and clean uniform and properly groomed. Reports to work properly equipped and physically and mentally fit to immediately assume duties.

Acceptable - Arrives for work on time. Uniform is neat, clean, pressed, tailored and properly worn. All leather gear, badge and other accessories are highly polished. Hair conforms to Division Standards. Always is properly equipped, and has necessary supplies and equipment to effectively perform daily duties. Arrives to work physically and mentally prepared to perform duties.

Responding - Arrives for work on time. Uniform is neat, clean. Leather gear, badge, and other accessories are clean and shined. Hair conforms to Division standards. Reports to duty properly equipped, and physically and mentally fit to assume duties. Generally possesses required paperwork and supplies to complete daily tasks. Requires only minor adjustment to uniform parts to be within policy.

Unacceptable - Arrives for work late. Uniform is not neat, clean, pressed and/or improperly worn. Leather gear and/or shoes are dirty. Hair is not groomed and does not conform to Division standards. PO displays poor hygiene and has offensive body odor/breath. Fails to report to duty properly equipped, physically/mentally fit and unable to immediately assume duties.
Roll Call/Cruiser Inspection – Evaluates ability to participate in roll calls, review Division issued material, and conduct proper inspection of equipment and cruiser in accordance with Patrol SOP.

Acceptable - Actively listens, participates, and communicates pertinent information in roll calls. Always reviews Daily Bulletins, Division e-mail, and other informational resources, and is able to processes the information and recall it as needed. Always conducts a thorough cruiser inspection at the beginning, during, and end of the tour of duty. Always inspects the passenger compartment upon exit of civilians, suspects, or prisoners.

Responding - Listens and participates in roll call. Generally reviews Daily Bulletins, Division e-mail, and other informational resources as required. Typically conducts a thorough cruiser inspection at the beginning, during, and end of tour of duty. Rarely needs to be reminded by FTO to inspect vehicle passenger compartment upon exit of civilians, suspects, or prisoners.

Unacceptable - Does not pay attention or participate in roll calls. Fails to review the Daily Bulletin, Division e-mail, or other informational resources as required. Has difficulty processing and/or recalling the information. Fails to conduct the required cruiser inspections at the beginning, during, and end of the tour of duty. Does not inspect vehicle passenger compartment upon exit of civilians, suspects, or prisoners.

2. Comprehension/Usage
Comprehension- Evaluates PO’s ability to communicate via radio (cruiser and portable), use Division computers and cruiser MPS.

Acceptable - Able to comprehend and effectively communicate via the cruiser and portable radio. Hears and acknowledges call number. Understands radio transmissions, and clearly conveys information. Has a working knowledge of the 10-code and phonetic alphabet. Transmissions are clear, complete and concise, containing all necessary information. Effectively and efficiently utilizes the various functions of computers and MPS. PO uses substation computer and MDC without assistance to accomplish necessary tasks.

Responding - Generally comprehends and effectively communicates via the cruiser and portable radio. Typically hears and acknowledges call number. Usually understands radio transmissions and clearly conveys information. Has a largely working knowledge of the 10-code and phonetic alphabet. Transmissions are typically clear, complete, concise, and contain all necessary information. Occasionally needs information repeated. Maintains and uses all commonly-used property and equipment to effectively perform assigned tasks. Is able to use substation computer and MDC functions with minimal FTO assistance and accepts information from other officers.

Unacceptable - Rarely hears and/or acknowledges call number. Fails to understand radio transmissions from dispatchers, supervisors and officers on the precinct/zone. Does not have a working knowledge of the 10-code or phonetic alphabet. Unable to effectively communicate via police radio. Frequently needs to have information repeated. Fails to maintain and use all commonly-used property and equipment to effectively perform assigned tasks. Is unable to use substation computer and MDC functions. Requires FTO to consistently provide direction and assistance.

Usage Skills – Evaluates PO’s ability to select and use appropriate cruiser/portable radio channels, various features of the radio system and the Mobile Data Computer (MPS) functions (LEADS, OHLEG, CAD etc.)
Acceptable - Understands and correctly uses the various radio channels and special features. (e.g., private call) Understand and uses the MPS functions without FTO assistance.
Responding - Has an understanding of and can use various radio channels and special features of the radio. Generally understands and uses the MPS functions, but requires minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable - Is unable to correctly use the various radio channels. Cannot use the radio’s special features, (e.g., private call). Unable to understand and use the MPS functions without FTO assistance.

3. Public/Police Interaction
Public Interaction – Evaluates ability to effectively interact, communicate, and display a professional demeanor with the general public.

Acceptable - Communicates with citizens by initiating contact, establishing a rapport and asks relevant questions pertaining to the situation. Presents a professional demeanor and treats others in an unbiased manner. Properly responds and provides required information.

Responding - Requires minimal FTO assistance to initiate contact and communicate with citizens. FTO assists with establishing a rapport and asking relevant questions pertaining to the situation. Presents a professional demeanor and treats others in an unbiased manner

Unacceptable - Fails to initiate contact and ineffectively communicates with citizens. Communicates in an abrupt or belligerent manner. Unable to establish a rapport and displays an introverted, biased or insensitive attitude. Requires FTO to intervene, deescalate and/or assume contact.
Police Interaction - Evaluates ability to effectively interact, communicate, and display a professional demeanor during contacts with peers, supervisors and civilian employees.

Acceptable - Effectively communicates and interacts with supervisors, sworn, and civilian employees. Understands and follows proper protocol and demonstrates proper respect towards peers and Chain of Command.

Responding - Capable of communicating with supervisors, sworn, and civilian employees, but requires FTO prompting or guidance. Generally understands and follows proper protocol and demonstrates proper respect towards peers and Chain of Command.

Unacceptable - Unable to effectively communicate and interact with supervisors, sworn, and civilian employees. Improperly addresses supervisors, sworn, and civilian employees, or does not display a respectful demeanor toward peers and Chain of Command. Fails to understand and follow proper protocol.
Verbal Conflict - Evaluates ability to gain and maintain control of situations through verbal command and instruction.

Acceptable - Demonstrates effective control of conflict through verbal communication and command. Able to restore order and deescalate conflict by adjusting voice inflection and tone. Uses proper word selection and comportment.
Responding - Capable of controlling conflict by speaking with authority in a calm, clear voice. Uses proper selection of words. Requires minimal FTO assistance to gain control.

Unacceptable - Unable to control conflict due to speaking in an inappropriate tone or using ineffective verbal communication. Exacerbates conflict with belligerent or improper comportment. Requires FTO intervention to gain control.
4. Feedback Acceptance
Feedback Acceptance –Evaluates the ability to accept feedback from FTO/supervisor. Demonstrates the ability to accept a critique of performance, knowledge or skills to further the learning process.

Acceptable - Actively solicits and accepts feedback or constructive criticism, and applies the information to further learning and improve performance. Does not rationalize mistakes or blame others for errors.
Responding - Generally solicits and accepts feedback or constructive criticism, and applies the information to further learning and improve performance. Rarely rationalizes mistakes.

Unacceptable - Fails to accept feedback or constructive criticism in a positive manner, and does not utilize the information to further learning and improve performance. Becomes argumentative, and/or deems it as a personal attack. Rationalizes mistakes or denies errors were made.

5. Precinct Orientation
Precinct Orientation – Evaluates the ability to familiarize themselves with the precinct, to remain alert to his/her present location, and to correctly use the city address numbering system.

Acceptable - Knows precinct boundaries, major roadways and landmarks. Clearly understands and correctly uses the city address numbering system. Recalls locations from previous calls for service and is consistently aware of his or her location.

Responding - Generally knows precinct boundaries, major roadways and landmarks. Understands the city address numbering system. Typically is aware of his/her present location and is able to find location with minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable- Unfamiliar with precinct boundaries, major roadways and landmarks. Does not understand the city address numbering system. Unaware of his or her present location. Unable to recall locations from previous calls for service. Requires FTO assistance with directions.
Response Time/Map Skills - Evaluates ability to arrive at determined destinations within an acceptable period of time and to effectively orient themselves and locate runs using maps.

Acceptable - Understands the importance of response time. Responds to calls for service in a timely manner. Demonstrates map reading skills, enabling him/her to consistently locate destinations by using the most direct route.

Responding - Generally arrives at destinations within a reasonable amount of time, demonstrates map reading skills and is able to locate destinations using the most direct route with minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable - Takes an inappropriate amount of time getting to destinations. Becomes disorientated and relies on FTO for assistance. Has difficulty finding locations by improperly using available maps and other resources or fails to employ maps when responding to calls for service.

6. Routine

Routine – Evaluates skill in the safe operation of the police vehicle under routine driving conditions. Ability to perform police related functions (radio communication, observation of vehicular and pedestrian traffic, computer usage, use of spotlight, etc.) while operating under normal conditions.
Acceptable - Operates vehicle in a safe, lawful and courteous manner. Displays defensive driving skills. Safely performs police related functions while operating a police vehicle.

Unacceptable - Operates vehicle in an unsafe manner, frequently violates traffic laws, or is discourteous to other motorists or pedestrians. Demonstrates poor defensive driving skills, and/or is not able to simultaneously perform police related functions.
7. EVO
Emergency/Pursuit – Evaluates skills in emergency vehicle operations and in pursuit driving situations. Exercises due regard to other vehicles/citizens.

Acceptable - Operates vehicle while exercising due regard in a competent and safe manner. Responds correctly to the degree of stress present. Correctly uses beacons and siren, monitors/conveys radio transmissions, observes surroundings and adheres to Policies and Directives during emergency or pursuit driving.

Unacceptable - Is apprehensive, fails to maintain control of the vehicle. Fails to practice defensive driving techniques. Demonstrates a disregard for the safety of themselves or others. Improperly uses beacons and siren, unable to monitor/convey radio transmissions, or observe surroundings. Fails to adhere to Policies and Directives during emergency or pursuit driving.

Policies/Procedures – Evaluates knowledge and application of Division Rules of Conduct, Policy Statements, Directives, SOP, etc., to various police related tasks, including reports and forms.

Acceptable - Displays a working knowledge of Division Rules, Directives, Policies and Procedures. Accurately recalls and applies Policies, Procedures and/or Directives relating to the duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment.

Responding - Displays basic working knowledge, is able to refer to and apply Division Rules, Directives, Policies and Procedures relating to the duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment with minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable - Does not display a basic working knowledge of Division Rules, Directives, Policies and Procedures. Unable to recall or apply Policies, Procedures or Directives relating to the duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment. Requires FTO assistance.
9. Criminal / Traffic Offenses

Criminal/Traffic Codes –Evaluates knowledge and application of the Ohio Revised Code, Columbus City Code, and State and City Traffic Codes. Capability of locating and selecting the proper enforcement code.

Acceptable - Consistently displays a general knowledge of the Ohio Revised Code and the Columbus City Code. Recognizes criminal and traffic offenses and understands the elements of each offense. Able to locate and select the correct section.

Responding - Generally displays a basic knowledge of the Ohio Revised Code and the Columbus City Code. Recognizes common criminal and traffic offenses and understands the elements of each offense. Requires minimal FTO assistance and direction with locating or selecting the correct section.

Unacceptable - Fails to display basic knowledge of the Ohio Revised Code and the Columbus City Code. Does not recognize common criminal and/or traffic offenses. Fails to understand the elements of each offense. Requires FTO assistance locating and selecting appropriate code.
10. Arrest, Search, Seizure
Arrest, Search, Seizure - Evaluates knowledge of Arrest, Search & Seizure manual and legal updates. Application of legal training and knowledge to patrol related situations.

Acceptable - Accurately applies laws relative to searching, seizing evidence, detaining persons, and effecting arrests while engaging in patrol duties. Demonstrates a knowledge and understanding of the Fourth Amendment.

Responding - Generally applies laws relative to searching, seizing evidence, detaining persons, and effecting arrests while engaging in patrol duties requiring minimal FTO assistance. Demonstrates a basic understanding of the Fourth Amendment.

Unacceptable - Fails to apply laws relative to searching, seizing evidence, detaining persons, and effecting arrests while engaging in patrol duties, requiring FTO assistance and direction. Fails to demonstrate a basic understanding of the Fourth Amendment.
11. Information Gathering
Policies/Procedures – Evaluates knowledge and application of Division Rules of Conduct, Policy Statements, Directives, SOP, etc., to various police related tasks, including reports and forms.

Acceptable - Displays a working knowledge of Division Rules, Directives, Policies and Procedures. Accurately recalls and applies Policies, Procedures and/or Directives relating to the duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment.

Responding - Displays basic working knowledge, is able to refer to and apply Division Rules, Directives, Policies and Procedures relating to the duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment with minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable - Does not display a basic working knowledge of Division Rules, Directives, Policies and Procedures. Unable to recall or apply Policies, Procedures or Directives relating to the duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment. Requires FTO assistance.
12. Resource/Equipment Usage

Resource Usage - Evaluates ability to utilize various resources and manuals to complete police related tasks (Traffic Crash Manual, Field Report Manual, OHLEG, Records, Accurint and other Units/Bureaus etc.).

Acceptable - Regularly and independently uses Law Enforcement related applications, reference sites and publications, and Division Manuals, both published and in electronic format, to assist in applying Policies, Procedures and/or Directives in the discharge of the PO’s duties and responsibilities of patrol assignment. PO consults with Detectives and other professionals both within and outside the Division to obtain guidance in the discharge of patrol duties.

Responding - Can independently use Law Enforcement related applications, reference sites and publications, and Division Manuals, both published and in electronic format, to assist in applying Policies, Procedures and/or Directives in the discharge of the PO’s duties and responsibilities of the patrol assignment with FTO prompting or minimal assistance. PO consults with Detectives and other professionals both within and outside the Division to obtain guidance in the discharge of patrol duties with minimal assistance or prompting from the FTO.

Unacceptable - Does not use Law Enforcement related applications, reference sites and publications, and Division Manuals, either published or in electronic format, to assist in applying Policies, Procedures and/or Directives in the discharge of the PO’s duties and responsibilities of the patrol assignment unless directed by, or with assistance from the FTO. PO fails to consult with Detectives and other professionals either within or outside the Division to obtain guidance in the discharge of patrol duties. Requires FTO direction or assistance.

Proper Usage of Equipment – Evaluates ability to use and maintain Division issued property and personally assigned equipment (e.g., service weapon, intermediate weapons, shotgun, flashlight, cruiser, breaching kit, crime scene tape, flares, and other necessary equipment.)
Acceptable - Properly maintains, inspects, and uses Division issued and personally assigned equipment and/or supplies to effectively perform daily patrol tasks.
Responding - Generally maintains, inspects, and uses all commonly-used property and equipment and/or supplies to effectively perform assigned tasks.
Unacceptable - Fails to maintain, inspect, and/or use Division issued and personally assigned equipment and/or supplies to effectively perform assigned tasks.
Official Reports
Official Report
13. Form Usage
Form Usage - Evaluates ability to properly select and utilize departmental forms necessary for task accomplishment.
Acceptable - Selects correct form. Familiar with all forms, including those lesser known and/or seldom used forms. Able to determine what forms, if any, are required to complete a particular task.
Responding - Generally selects the appropriate form for a particular task. Knows the commonly used forms and understands their usage needing minimal FTO assistance.
Unacceptable - Fails to select the correct form to be completed and/or is unable to select and complete the proper form for the given situation.
14. Grammar/Legibility

Grammar/Legibility - Evaluates ability to use correct spelling, proper grammar (e.g. sentence structure, punctuation, etc.) and is able to neatly complete forms, using legible, easy-to-read block printing.

Acceptable - Written reports contain no spelling or grammatical errors. Narratives are concise and easily understood. Completed forms are very neat and legible. Block printing is always evenly spaced and easy to read.

Responding - Written reports generally contain proper grammar, sentence structure and spelling with few errors that do not detract from narrative clarity and content. Completed forms are neat using block printing and consistent spacing. Error corrections are completed in a neat manner. Completed with minimal FTO assistance

Unacceptable - Written reports contain an excessive number of misspelled words. Sentence structure and word usage is improper and/or incomplete. Narratives present information in a disorganized manner. Reports are illegible. Printing is unevenly spaced and difficult to read. Reports lack overall neatness. Erasure marks or white-outs are visible. Errors are corrected by scratching out or writing over original information.
15. Content Accuracy
Content Accuracy - Evaluates ability to complete reports that accurately reflect the incident being reported in a detailed, thorough, and organized manner.

Acceptable - Reports display a high degree of content accuracy. Reports are a complete, detailed and provide a chronological account of events. They are written and organized in an understandable manner. No pertinent details or facts are omitted.

Responding - Generally completes reports in an organized and chronological manner. Reports contain required information and details and are completed with reasonable accuracy and thoroughness. Requires minimal FTO input or direction.
Unacceptable - Unable to organize information. Pertinent details or facts are omitted. Reports are incomplete and inaccurate. Requires FTO to rewrite or dictate the narrative portion of reports.
16. Completion Time

Completion Time - Evaluates the amount of time taken to complete Division forms/reports relative to the nature and level of complexity of the incident. Note: other factors such as processing scenes, processing through ID Unit, arrival of detectives or wreckers, transports to hospitals, etc. shall be taken into consideration when determining completion time.
Acceptable - Able to accurately and thoroughly complete forms/reports in an amount of time expected of a patrol officer.
Responding - Completes forms/reports with an acceptable degree of accuracy and in a reasonable amount of time expected of a one officer patrol unit with minimal FTO assistance and direction.

Unacceptable - Requires an excessive amount of time to complete forms/reports. Finished paperwork is still incomplete and inaccurate. Requires FTO assistance. (Note: FTO must document the total amount of time taken to complete forms when using this rating.)
