17. Response to Enforcement
Criminal Violations - Evaluates ability to recognize criminal violations and intervene while on routine patrol and take appropriate enforcement action.
Acceptable - Recognizes criminal activity and takes appropriate enforcement action with no FTO direction.
Responding - Recognizes most obvious criminal violations and usually is able to take action with a minimum of FTO direction.
Unacceptable - Does not recognize obvious criminal violations or fails to take action without FTO direction.
Traffic Enforcement - Evaluates ability to recognize and take appropriate action on traffic violations.
Acceptable - Recognizes traffic violations and takes appropriate action with no FTO direction.
Responding - Recognizes most traffic violations and takes appropriate action with a minimum of FTO direction.
Unacceptable - Does not recognize obvious traffic violations or fails to take action without FTO direction.
Suspicious Activity - Evaluates ability to recognize and take appropriate action in response to suspicious activity

Acceptable - Remains alert and is aware of surroundings and recognizes suspicious activity. Takes appropriate action, conducts record/warrant checks and completes field interviews on suspicious persons
Responding - Remains aware of surroundings and recognizes obvious suspicious activity. Generally observes obvious suspicious activity. Takes appropriate action with little assistance from FTO.
Unacceptable - Does not notice obvious suspicious activity. Does not take appropriate action after observing suspicious activity. Requires direction and assistance from FTO.
Officer Safety

Due to the complexity and extreme importance of the officer safety categories, a guide of accepted officer procedures is listed below. This list is not all-inclusive. Failure to follow any of the below listed practices will result in an unacceptable performance rating for the day.
Does not expose weapons to suspect (baton, mace, firearm, etc.).
Keeps gun hand free during enforcement situations.
Does not stand in front of traffic violator’s vehicle door. Does not stand in front of entry doors to buildings/residences (fatal funnel).
Controls suspect’s movements.
Keeps violator/suspect in sight.
Uses necessary and proper illumination.
Utilizes/maintains personal safety equipment.
Anticipates potentially dangerous situations.
Does not stand too close to passing vehicular traffic.
Is careful and deliberate in handling firearms and other weapons.
Makes a reasonable choice of which weapon to use and when to use it.
Covers other officers.
Does not stand or walk between violators and police vehicle during vehicle stops.
Searches police vehicle prior to duty, after each prisoner/citizen transport and at end of tour. Also applies to performance category #1.
Completes a thorough, systematic 2/3 search following handcuffing of an arrestee or prior to transporting a prisoner
Conducts a thorough, systematic pat-down for weapons, when allowed by law and recognizes when the case law applies.
18. Threat Assessment

Unknown Threat Contacts - Evaluates ability to demonstrate accepted and trained officer safety techniques when initiating contact(s). Evaluates and assesses situation to determine if any possible threat exists.

Acceptable - Exercises and maintains proper/trained officer safety techniques/skills at all times. Uses accepted officer safety skills/tactics to safely initiate contacts. Recognizes dangers/threats and reacts appropriately.

Unacceptable - Does not exercise or maintain proper/trained officer safety techniques/skills at all times. Fails to use and apply proper officer safety skills/tactics to safely initiate contacts. Unaware of danger/threats and does not react appropriately. Requires FTO assistance and direction.

Known Threat Contacts - Evaluates ability to recognize and respond to known threats when approaching locations, structures and others. Demonstrates accepted and trained officer safety techniques when responding to calls for service involving known threats.

Acceptable - Exercises and maintains proper/trained officer safety techniques/skills upon recognizing or responding to situations involving a known threat. Can perceive and recognize a threat and uses accepted officer safety techniques to control and stop the threat.

Unacceptable - Does not exercise proper/trained officer safety techniques. Requires FTO assistance and direction to perceive and recognize a threat, is unable to use accepted officer safety techniques to control and stop the threat. Lacks basic understanding of the necessity of officer safety skills or becomes too relaxed upon determination of a non-existing threat.
19. Initiating Arrests
Initiating Arrests - Evaluates ability to maintain accepted and trained officer safety skills and techniques while initiating arrests.

Acceptable - Exercises and maintains proper/trained officer safety techniques/skills and control while initiating arrests. Effectively controls prisoner, applies handcuffs and escorts to a safe location to perform search incident to arrest. Handcuffs prisoner prior to conducting search and secures prisoner in cruiser.

Unacceptable - Does not use proper/trained officer safety techniques/skills and control while initiating arrests. Lacks knowledge and assertiveness to initiate arrests. Requires FTO assistance and/or direction when controlling prisoners, applying handcuffs and escorting to a safe location to perform search incident to arrest. Does not handcuff prisoner prior to searching or placing prisoner in cruiser.
20. Handling Prisoners
Handling Prisoners - Evaluates ability to transport prisoners in a safe, effective manner using trained officer safety skills.

Acceptable - Uses proper/trained officer safety skills and monitors/observes prisoner’s movements. Conducts search whenever custody of a prisoner is transferred from another officer. Checks cruiser for contraband/weapons after transport of each prisoner. Seatbelts prisoners prior to transport. Does not permit prisoners to communicate during transport. Takes precautions to prevent escape and safely processes prisoners. Uses appropriate verbal commands and displays command bearing.

Unacceptable - Does not use proper/trained officer safety skills. Fails to follow Division Policy addressing prisoner transport. Does not monitor prisoner’s movement and/or maintain physical control to prevent escape. Does not use appropriate verbal commands to convey instructions to prisoner. Requires FTO assistance and direction.
21. Vehicle Stops
Vehicle Stops - Evaluates ability to conduct vehicle stops using trained officer safety standards, to include high risk stops.

Acceptable - Uses proper/trained officer safety skills while initiating or during vehicle stops. Airs traffic stop information. Properly positions cruiser. Safely and systematically approaches vehicle. Observes and controls movements of occupants. Retrieves required information/documents. Provides clear verbal instructions and uses flashlight.

Unacceptable - Does not use proper/trained officer safety skills while initiating or during vehicle stops. Fails to air traffic stop information, properly position cruiser, or safely and systematically approach vehicle. Requires FTO assistance and/or direction to control movements of occupants, retrieving required information/documents and complete other required tasks of completing stop.
22. Run Approach

Approach/Inside Structures - Evaluates ability to approach the structure using proper/trained officer safety techniques. Evaluates ability to apply trained building search tactics and maintain an awareness of potential threats while inside the structure. (Includes building searches as well as calls for service involving officer safety in and/or around a structure)

Acceptable - Uses proper/trained officer safety techniques by parking away from the structure, observing suspicious activity/persons, using appropriate cover, communicating with partner, and making safe entry. Properly utilizes flashlight/weapon. Methodically clears interior of structures and safely secures any possible suspects. Maintains environmental awareness of potential threats while handling calls for service in/or around structures.

Unacceptable - Fails to demonstrate proper/trained officer safety skills. Places self or others in danger by not safely and tactically approaching/clearing structures. Fails to properly utilize flashlight and weapon. Fails to maintain environmental awareness of potential threats.
23. Building Search

Approach/Inside Structures - Evaluates ability to approach the structure using proper/trained officer safety techniques. Evaluates ability to apply trained building search tactics and maintain an awareness of potential threats while inside the structure. (Includes building searches as well as calls for service involving officer safety in and/or around a structure)

Acceptable - Uses proper/trained officer safety techniques by parking away from the structure, observing suspicious activity/persons, using appropriate cover, communicating with partner, and making safe entry. Properly utilizes flashlight/weapon. Methodically clears interior of structures and safely secures any possible suspects. Maintains environmental awareness of potential threats while handling calls for service in/or around structures.

Unacceptable - Fails to demonstrate proper/trained officer safety skills. Places self or others in danger by not safely and tactically approaching/clearing structures. Fails to properly utilize flashlight and weapon. Fails to maintain environmental awareness of potential threats.
24. Pat Down/Searches
Pat Down/Searches - Evaluates ability to safely and thoroughly perform pat down/ search.

Acceptable- Capable of performing a Terry pat down or search using proper/trained officer safety skills. Completes a thorough and systematic pat down or search. Locates all weapons, contraband and/or personal property. Complies with Division Policy when conducting pat down/search.

Unacceptable - Does not use proper/trained officer safety skills when conducting a pat down/search. Fails to conduct a thorough and systematic pat down/search, does not locate weapons, contraband, and/or personal property.
Judgment Decisions
25. Low Stress Situations

Low Stress Situation - Evaluates ability to assess an incident and choose an appropriate course of action in routine, low-stress police activities. Capable of handling, managing, and resolving calls for service or self-initiated runs.

Acceptable - Properly assesses incidents which may involve routine or complex matters. Determines an appropriate and reasonable course of action. Demonstrates an ability to identify problems and determine a resolution.

Responding - Generally assesses routine incidents and determines the appropriate and reasonable course of action. Demonstrates an ability to identify problems and determine a resolution with minimal FTO assistance.
Unacceptable - Unable to properly assess routine incidents. Fails to identify problems or determine a resolution. Relies on FTO to determine proper course of action.
26. High Stress Situations

Stress Situations - Evaluates ability to choose an appropriate course of action in moderate and high-stress incidents. Capable of recognizing, controlling and resolving calls for service or self-initiated activities.

Acceptable - Remains calm and demonstrates self-control in moderate and high stress incidents. Determines the appropriate course of action to restore order. Demonstrates a proper degree of decisiveness.
Responding - Usually remains calm and demonstrates self-control in moderate and high stress incidents. Determines the appropriate course of action to restore order with minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable - Unable to remain calm and demonstrate self-control in moderate and high stress incidents. Fails to determine the best course of action. Makes poor decisions or no decision at all. FTOs assistance is required to restore order.
27. Arrest Situations
Arrest Situations - Evaluates decision-making ability and use of judgment when confronted with an arrest situation.
Acceptable - Displays ability to assess and identify an arrest situation. Capable of assessing information and making a decision to effect an arrest. Demonstrates a proper degree of decisiveness.
Responding - Usually displays the ability to assess and identify an arrest situation. Capable of assessing information and making a decision to effect an arrest with minimal FTO assistance.
Unacceptable - Unable to assess and identify an arrest situation. Has difficulty assessing information and making a decision to effect an arrest. Depends on FTO for appropriate course of action.
28. Problem Solving
Problem Solving - Evaluates PO’s ability to perceive and form valid conclusions. Measures the PO’s ability to exercise sound judgment and make proper decisions.
Acceptable- Demonstrates problem-solving abilities, exercises sound judgment and decision making abilities. Correctly contacts or refers citizens to the appropriate outside agencies.
Responding- Capable of reasoning through a problem and arrives at acceptable conclusion. Contacts or refers citizens to the appropriate outside agencies with minimal FTO assistance.

Unacceptable - Unable to reason through a problem and reach a conclusion. Makes improper referrals or fails to make referrals. Relies on FTO’s assistance and direction to refer citizens to the appropriate outside agency.
29. Motivational Traits
Motivational Traits - Evaluates ability to act independently of FTO, demonstrates assertiveness and determination while projecting a positive demeanor.
Acceptable - Displays an eagerness to volunteer for dispatched calls and/or engage in self-initiated activity by completing daily patrol tasks and assisting fellow officers.
Responding - Engages in dispatched and/or self-initiated activity by completing daily patrol tasks and assisting fellow officers. However, consults FTO prior to taking action.
Unacceptable - Lacks assertiveness or fails to engage in dispatched or self-initiated activity. Rationalizes lack of action or indecisiveness. Frequently relies on FTO to take charge.
30. Task Management
Multitasking - Evaluates ability to safely and effectively perform multiple police-related tasks simultaneously.
Acceptable - Capable of safely and effectively performing multiple police-related tasks simultaneously.
Responding - Capable of safely and effectively performing multiple police-related tasks simultaneously requiring minimal FTO assistance to remain focused.
Unacceptable - Unable to safely and effectively perform multiple police-related tasks simultaneously. Requires significant FTO assistance to remain focused.

The Weekly Performance Summary (U10.174)

Upon completion of each training week, the FTO will submit a Weekly Performance Summary. The Weekly Performance Summary is a “net result” of the week’s activity and training. This summary will provide documentation regarding the probationary officer’s strengths, weaknesses, and total time of corrective training for the week by performance category. The FTO will complete a Weekly Performance Summary for each completed work week of all training phases. The Weekly Performance Summary consists of the following four documentation areas:

 Performance Categories: The Excel Program will automatically complete this section by totaling the check marks in each corresponding performance category for the Daily Performance Summaries and placing this total in the corresponding performance category box on the Weekly Performance Summary.

 Weekly Activity Summary: The Excel Program will total the Daily Performance Summaries and record the total in the corresponding activity in numeric form. This will assist in the review of the PO’s weekly activity and indicate areas that need attention in the upcoming training week.

 Weekly Comment/Signature: This form is used as an acknowledgment of the PO’s review of the weekly packet and any additional comments. The FTO will briefly comment on the PO’s overall performance, and address and areas that are of concern.

 Probationary Officer Weekly Performance Log: This form will be used to address PO’s Strengths and Deficient Performance Areas. Any category in which the PO received an “Unacceptable” or “Not Responding to Training” rating shall be noted here, along with the corrective training provided by the FTO and the amount of time spent on the corrective training.
Assembling a Weekly Evaluation Packet

The FTO will complete and upload all completed Weekly Evaluation Packets to the FTO Office in a timely fashion (within 3 days after the end of a workweek), in accordance with the guidelines set forth in the Field Training Report Completion Guide. The Weekly Evaluation should be reviewed by the PO prior to it being uploaded to the FTO Drive (I:) for conversion by the FTO Office.
A Weekly Evaluation Packet shall include the following items prior to being reviewed by the PO:
Weekly Performance Summary
 Weekly Performance Log
 Daily Performance Summary (a summary for each day)
Weekly Comment/Signature Form
 FTO Daily Checklist Reports (Reporting for Duty, Call for Service, Traffic Stop, High Risk Stop, Building Search, Traffic Crash Investigation and/or Domestic Incident)
 FTO Supplemental Checklist forms (Narrative Addition Form, Arrest Process, OVI Process, Substation/Headquarters/Court Orientation)
 Any additional supplements (e.g., Documentation Summary, copies of completed reports and forms, completed tests used for training, etc.)

text: Please refer to the “Daily Activity Summary Definitions” to correctly complete each field. This area is used to maintain statistics on how many times a PO completes a specific form/report or completed a certain patrol activity. This section is to be completed each day of training, including Limbo Days.
Daily Activity Summary- Definitions
PremierOne Reports
The total number of incident reports taken during the shift. In this section, do not include Traffic Crash Reports, U-10.100s, or FI reports.
FI Reports

The total number of FI reports taken during the shift. Also, if a person is arrested, and the probationary officer transfers custody to another jurisdiction instead of slating, an FI report is generated rather than a PremierOne Report.
Accident Reports
The total number of Traffic Crash Reports completed during the shift. Do not count an accident as a PremierOne Report.
Impound Slips
The total number of Impound Slips completed during a shift.
PC Affidavits
The total number of PC Affidavits completed during a shift.
Property Slips

The number of Property Slips completed during a shift. This does not include any other property room forms or requests. The FTO’s name and badge number should be placed on all Property Slips during Field Training.
Traffic Stops

The number of Non-Traffic Crash stops conducted during the shift to include, motor vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle stops/offenses. Note that motor vehicle stops will be completed on a Traffic Stop form and Pedestrian Stops will be completed on a Self-Initiated Run/Training form.
Traffic Citations

The number of traffic citation forms completed, not the number of listed offenses. This includes citations issued for motor vehicle traffic stops, traffic crashes, pedestrian, and bicycle stops. For example, if a driver ran a stop sign and did not possess a valid license, this would count as one traffic citation.
Parking Citations
The number of parking citations completed during a shift.
First Responder Letters
The total number of First Responder Letters completed during the shift, regardless of the format.
The number of Arrest Reports completed during the shift. This section does not include PremierOne Offense or Incident Reports.
Criminal Complaints
The number of Criminal Complaint Forms completed during the shift. This includes Adult misdemeanor and felony, and Juvenile (JU5302/eJU5302) delinquent and unruly complaints.
Misdemeanor Summons

The number of misdemeanor citations or summonses issued during the shift. These are not counted as misdemeanor arrest since the person was released at scene. The number should represent the number of criminal complaints issued in which the person was provided a court date and not slated.
Misdemeanor Arrests

The number of misdemeanor arrests for both on-view and warrants. Also, if a misdemeanor warrant was filed for a person’s arrest. Count one arrest for each person arrested, regardless of the number of charges/warrants filed. If a person is arrested for both on-view and warrant, count the arrest under the higher charge. If the person is arrested for both misdemeanor and felony charges, count the arrest under the “Felony Arrests” category. Misdemeanor Citations/Summonses do not count as an arrest. Rather, Misdemeanor Citations/ Summonses are entered in the “Misdemeanor Summons” Category. A prisoner who is refused at the jail for medical reasons would be counted toward the number of misdemeanor arrests.
Felony Packet/Direct Ind.
The total number of felony packets or Direct Indictment packets completed by the Probationary Officer. Does not to include packets by Detectives.
Felony Arrests

The number of felony arrests for both on-view and warrant arrests. Includes felony warrants filed for an individual’s arrest. Count one arrest for each person arrested regardless of the number of charges/warrants filed. If a person is arrested for both on-view and on-warrant, count the arrest under the higher charge. If a person is arrested for both misdemeanor and felony charges, count the arrest under the “Felony Arrests” category. If the prisoner is refused at the jail for medical, then it still counts toward the number of felony arrest.
DV Packets
The number of DV Packets completed during the shift. Packets may be for warrants filed, or on-view arrests. One packet per arrestee.
OVI Packets
The number of OVI Packets completed during the shift.
Prisoners Slated
The number of persons arrested and slated. If the person is refused at the jail, it still counts toward the number of prisoners slated.
Completed Payouts

The number of persons detained for active warrants who are later transported to the Clerk of Courts to pay fines/fees in lieu of being slated. Payouts should not be counted as misdemeanor arrests, unless the payout is not or cannot be completed, and the person is slated on the verified warrant(s).
Suspicious Person Stops
The total number of investigatory stops or consensual encounters (non-traffic related) conducted by the Probationary Officer during the shift.
Prisoner Searches
The total number of searches of an individual’s person conducted by the Probationary Officer during the shift, to be differentiated from the execution of pat downs.
Pat Downs
The total number of pat downs of an individual’s person conducted by the Probationary Officer during the shift, to be differentiated from the execution of a search.
Attempted/Warrants Served

The process of training the Probationary Officer in proactively seeking out specific individuals with warrants, verifying, and serving, or attempting to serve the warrants. This section is used to count the number of individuals proactively sought out and/or arrested rather than the number of warrants served. This category counts arrests or attempted arrests stemming from dispatched calls for service or self-initiated activity related solely to searching for individuals with active arrest warrants (10-50/10-50A). This section is not used to count the number of individuals arrested stemming from other dispatched or self-initiated activities, such as traffic or suspicious person stops.

Week 15 Recommendation

The FTO Program is a 15 week program divided into four (4) phases. During Phase I, II, and III, the PO will automatically be assigned to the next phase unless a recommendation is made to cease training. After completing Phase IV, the assigned FTO will make a recommendation to release the PO to the Probationary Phase, or to not release the PO to the Probationary Phase. In extreme cases, a PO may be deemed incompetent, incapable, or unwilling to perform required duties. A recommendation to cease training may be made at any point during training. Documentation must support all recommendations to cease training. In such cases, the FTO Sergeant and Field Training Board will review all documentation and take the necessary action.

The Phase IV FTO is required to make a recommendation concerning release from the Field Training Program. The recommendation will be made on the Weekly Performance Summary of Week 15. The recommendation will be documented on the Weekly Packet Acknowledgement Form (Comment Signature) in the “Field Training Officer Comments” section using the following verbiage:

“On Phase four PO _______ demonstrated they could perform at an acceptable level in the 38 categories that make up the Standard Evaluation Guidelines and have shown they can operate as a safe efficient one officer unit with little to no FTO assistance.”
-or-

“On Phase four PO­­­­_______ did not demonstrate they could perform at an acceptable level in the 38 categories that make up the Standard Evaluation Guidelines and have not shown they can operate as a safe efficient one officer car without significant FTO assistance.”
***The FTO Office must be made aware in advance any time a Phase IV FTO plans to recommend a PO not be released to the Probationary Phase.***

FTOs in all four phases should be proactive in the thorough documentation of deficient PO performance, especially of such a repetitive nature as to merit an “NRT” rating. FTOs should also notify the FTO Office regarding such performance as soon as possible so as to permit intervention - and the documentation of such interventions - during a PO’s training.

The Phase IV FTO, immediately upon suspecting that a PO’s consistently deficient performance could lead to a recommendation of termination, should notify the FTO Office in order to ensure such recommendation is adequately supported by documentation, and to obtain guidance from the FTO Office in proceeding.

Creating and Using Digital Signatures
About Digital Signatures

Adobe Acrobat supports a range of electronic and digital signature solutions – including certificate signatures that let you sign PDF files with a certificate-based digital ID. Digital signatures can be used on documents that support them, such as the Comment and Signature form.
What is a digital signature?
A digital signature is an electronic proof of a person’s identity involving the use of encryption authenticate documents.
Adobe Acrobat can be used so that end-users can create their own certificate IDs. This enables personnel to sign and validate documents digitally.
Why use certificate signatures?

Many business transactions, including financial, legal and other regulated transactions, require high assurance when signing documents. When documents are distributed electronically, it is important that recipients can:
Verify document authenticity - confirming the identity of each person who signed the document.
Verify document integrity - confirming that the document has not been altered in transit Certificate-based signatures provide both of these security services.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: The PO was dispatched on an information/assistance run. The PO used computer map and gave the FTO directions to the scene. The PO gave the most direct route. The PO met the caller and performed a thorough preliminary investigation with no assistance from the FTO. The PO obtained appropriate information and decided to file a Menacing Report. The PO provided the caller with the incident number and referred her to the Court of Domestic Relations to file charges on the juvenile suspect is she learned the juvenile’s name. The PO relocated to a secure location and completed the incident report with minimal FTO assistance. The PO’s report contained an error. The PO listed the report disposition as “1-Exception.” The PO did not have the suspect’s full name. The FTO had PO change the disposition top “4-Active.” The FTO told the PO that “1-Exception” was used when enough information about the suspect was known to file charges.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: FTO and PO were dispatched with another unit to the report of a domestic situation involving a gun. FTO discussed with PO why and how to meet up with other responding units while en route to the meeting location. The caller did not show up so all units responded to the possible incident location. FTO demonstrated to PO how to interview the female half who was very calm and stated there was no violence and her boyfriend already left. FTO demonstrated to PO on how to use the communications channel to contact the caller who then provided a third location of where he would be. FTO and PO drove to the male half who originally claimed there was a gun involved and violence but changed his story. FTO demonstrated to PO on how to refer the male to the prosecutor's office for further assistance and provided the incident report number. PO completed a report documenting the situation and why charges were not filed with FTO assistance before clearing.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: PO responded to a drug overdose with another unit. PO responded utilizing emergency vehicle operations due to the distance away from the location. PO was driving eastbound on Sullivant Ave behind the other officer who was also utilizing EVO. PO approached the intersection of Sullivant Ave and S Hague Ave with a red light. Traffic on S Hague Ave with the green light was still stopped from the other cruiser in front of PO. PO touched the brake before he reached the intersection but failed to stop and ensure the intersection was clear to cross. At the conclusion of the run FTO reviewed with PO how to safely drive using EVO and PO stated he understood his mistake after reviewing the cruiser video. PO arrived as the medics entered and revived the unconscious male suffering from an overdose. PO did an acceptable job speaking with the caller, collecting information and checking for warrants. The male refused to be transported by medics and was left at scene. PO completed the necessary report with minimal FTO assistance at a later time in the shift.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: PO was dispatched to the listed location about a neighbor dispute that started from a dog peeing in the yard. PO arrived and spoke to the caller first. Meanwhile, the neighbor also came out onto her porch to join in the talk. PO asked the female to wait until he was finished talking with the first neighbor. The female complied and waited a moment then joined in the conversation in a mature/helpful way. PO listened to her and helped mediate a resolution between the neighbors.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: PO and another unit were dispatched on a report of a person who was having a dispute with neighbors. PO arrived and parked in a safe location. The other unit already made contact, and called for an MCR Unit (Mobile Crisis Response Unit). PO talked with the female and gathered information. PO then talked with MCR when they arrived. PO then communicated with EMS when they arrived. PO used good and appropriate force to hold the female and wait for EMS. PO then advised radio of the Medic and transport location. PO cleared via radio.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: PO was dispatched on a report of a motor vehicle theft. PO drove a direct route and noted the caller was not at scene. PO then used Comm Channel and found the caller was near the location. PO located the caller and initiated contact PO gathered needed information for a report. PO noted that the caller did not know the tag, only had a picture of VIN. PO used the Records Channel and verified the vehicle was blank for Impound. Repo. PO gathered needed/ available information for a report. PO gave the caller the incident number. PO completed a Premier-1 report with all information. PO completed a good detailed narrative. PO cleared via radio.

section: FTO Call for Service: Example Narratives
text: P.O. was dispatched with another officer on a call of a domestic, stand by while she gathered clothing. P.O. used acceptable radio skills and drove to the run. P.O. found both parties involved and used acceptable interpersonal skills. The female half stated she wanted to get some clothes out of the house that belonged to her. The male half stated that she moved out three months ago with all her stuff. A landlord was present to verify the male half story and FTO was at scene when she moved all her stuff out. The male half stated that the female had nothing left and refused to let her in to check. P.O. advised the female that since she moved out she is no longer to walk in without the male’s permission and she would have to leave. P.O. cleared the run.

P.O. used acceptable interpersonal skills and spoke with the medics and nurses that were dealing with the victim in the trauma room. P.O. was able to determine that this was most likely a domestic violence report. P.O. gathered more information and found that the assault was felonious. P.O. contacted CHOICES and had the victim talk with them on the phone. The detective asked P.O. and FTO to stay at the hospital and wait for a list of the victim’s injuries and try to convince her to give the suspect information so he could file charges. The male told the officers that several different police agencies had been to his house to look for the wanted person, but the suspect had never actually lived at the residence. section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives
text: PO observed a pedestrian violation (jaywalking) at the above listed location and stopped the violator. PO safely positioned the cruiser, activated the overhead lights, and advised radio of his location and run type. PO displayed good reactionary gap and interview stance while he spoke with the male. PO gathered the male’s ID and performed the necessary checks. PO decided the best course of action would be to issue the male a warning. PO issued the warning and released the male from the scene. PO classified the CVS recording and cleared C-2V over the MDC/radio.

section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives
text: (Training) In response to some questions and comments raised by PO, FTO reviewed Division Directive 3.03 in regards to searching subjects of the opposite sex. FTO explained the cases, PO should perform these actions at the hood of the cruiser with the CVS and BWC activated. FTO also explained that PO should not perform any kind of pat down using the back of his hand because it is extremely difficult to discern the identity of objects using this method. FTO reviewed the Field Report Manual, section 2.11. FTO explained the proper procedure for completing an arrest repot arising from warrants filed from an existing CPD case. FTO demonstrated the process of completing a “.2” document on a Premiere One. PO stated he believed he understood the process.

section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives

Officers then noted the suspects were walking from the rear to the front of the business. When officers pulled in front, both suspects saw officers and split up. FTO then initiated contact, PO noted the 1 male kept his hands in his pocket and requested he keep his hands out of his pocket. FTO conducted a pat down. FTO talked with 1 male and gathered his information. PO talked with the other male, and never gathered his information. PO did not mark with radio her location, FTO, while in contact with 1 of the individuals marked with radio their location. Later, FTO asked PO where they were and PO was unable to tell FTO where she was. PO cleared via radio.

section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives

FTO and PO saw the male walk into the parking lot and behind a fence. FTO advised PO of the male's information and that he was trespassed. PO then drove around the block, not turning around in the parking lot and look for the male, losing sight of him. PO drove the area and did not locate him. PO thought maybe he went in a building where he was last seen. PO marked with radio her correct location and walked the building, unable to locate the male. PO cleared via radio.

section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives

FTO advised P.O. the warrants were good and she stopped, aired her location and made a safe approach. P.O. advised the male he had a warrant for his arrest, gave him loud verbal commands and placed the male in handcuffs, completed a pat down while FTO searched. P.O placed the male in the rear of the cruiser, activated the CVS and buckled the male in his seat. P.O. completed the necessary paperwork and followed prisoner transport procedures. P.O. cleared the jail and took some property to the property room. P.O. cleared code 3 over the radio.

section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives

FTO had to remind PO at this time to mark his stop and location with radio. FTO advised PO he needs to always notify radio of all stops for officer safety reasons. After placing the female under arrest for the warrant, a search performed by FTO recovered a needle. FTO discussed the situation with PO and with assistance was able to determine he needed to read the female her rights to determine what she uses the needle for. PO read the female her rights and she quickly advised she uses it to inject heroin. FTO advised PO to complete the paperwork in a safe location and he transported the female arrestee to an area near the substation. PO failed to advise radio of the transport. FTO advised PO he needs to notify radio of all transports and he stated he understood his mistake. PO was able to determine the necessary paperwork that needed completed with some FTO assistance. FTO assisted PO in organizing his method of completing the paperwork and multitasking. PO completed the paperwork with some FTO assistance. FTO assisted PO in organizing the arrest summary in a logical manner and adding detail to document the fresh charges. PO completed the ticket and criminal complaint with minimal assistance. PO completed the probable cause affidavit with some FTO assistance. PO used acceptable prisoner transport procedures in transporting the female to HQ for ID, clerks and then to FCJ II. The female was medically refused from the jail and PO transported her to Grant Hospital where she was treated. Once released from the hospital, PO transported the female back to jail where she was slated. PO transported the needle to the property room for evidence. PO completed a prisoner hospital transport report with FTO assistance before clearing the run with radio.

section: FTO Self-Initiated Run / Training: Example Narratives

PO turned around and confirmed it was a beer and FTO instructed PO to speak with her. PO collected the identification of the female and determined she did not have any warrants. PO completed a criminal complaint for the charge with minimal FTO assistance. PO issued the citation to the female with FTO assistance and collected a sample of the beer. PO completed the arrest paperwork with some FTO assistance. The content of the report was much improved from previous reports but took an unacceptable amount of time to complete. PO still needs to make sure he checks his reports for grammatical errors and typos. PO completed the property slip and probable cause affidavit with some FTO assistance before sending it via matrix. PO submitted the sample of beer to the property room and cleared the run with radio.

PO and another unit were dispatched on a report of a domestic dispute, the caller wanted her boyfriend to leave and hung up the phone. PO located the run and planned her approach. PO then drove a direct route, when close, PO thought she was on the wrong street, PO was on the correct street and started to ask FTO for help. PO then drove past the street she needed to turn down. PO then noticed that she was on the correct street and was able to re-orient herself. PO then located the dispatched address and noted that she was in front. PO continued past, turned around, parked, and made a safe approach. PO attempted contact, but got no answer. PO noted she could not hear anything. PO used Comm Channel and was advised the caller left. PO cleared the scene and cleared via radio.

PO and another unit were dispatched on a report of an ex-husband, who was outside and refusing to leave. PO drove down Shanley and pulled onto Alona Dr. PO noted that she was on the wrong street and was slow to decide to turn around and then continued down Shanley Dr. PO slowly drove down Shanley and stopped, unsure of where the dispatched location was. PO then noticed that she was getting closer and parked in safe location. PO made a safe approach and initiated contact with the caller. PO talked with the caller and gathered some information. PO asked some questions and the caller gave PO a Protection Order. While PO initiated contact, FTO noted a neighbor, was a witness and had good information. PO asked the caller if the male/ husband was on the lease or lived with her. The caller was unable to understand and requested a Nepali interpreter. PO with some assistance called and used the language line. PO then got questions answered. PO, FTO and the other unit talked with a 10 year old, who also was a witness and had information about the incident. PO then talked with the neighbor, who advised the ex was there and has been showing up every time the current male/ husband is out. PO decided to complete a Premier-1 report and nothing further. FTO stopped PO and advised that she was Probable Cause and should file a warrant on the file. FTO explained that violating a protection order and having a probable cause, the preferred course of action is to file a warrant or make an arrest. PO contacted Records to verify the protection Order. While talking with PO and getting ready to clear the scene, FTO saw the suspect ( FTO knew the suspect from previous arrests) PO approached the male, the male saw officers approach and started to walk away, PO quickly moved to the suspect, placing him under arrest. FTO assisted by conducting a search for PO. PO then advised radio she had an arrest. PO then changed her location and completed a Premier-1 report. PO's narrative was detailed with no errors. PO's U-10-100 had errors. PO added the protection order's case in the offense's case box of her U-10-100. FTO explained that the case number is when she gathers a case number from the clerk's office or is a case number from a warrant. FTO then had to advise PO she needed to complete a Criminal Complaint and PC Affidavit. PO was able to locate the correct code and wording, using her red book. PO then advised she was en-route to the clerk's. FTO had to advise PO that she needed to process the arrestee through the Identification Unit, later PO and FTO reviewed Directive. During the next day, PO was able to locate the Directive that stated reasons an officer would need to process a person through the Identification Unit. PO changed with radio her location and drove a direct route to headquarter to process the arrestee through the Identification Unit. While in the sally port, the arrestee refused to exit the cruiser and follow through with the arrest process. FTO advised PO that they will not process him through the Identification Unit due to his behavior and being extremely intoxicated. PO then changed her location to the clerk's office. While en route, PO drove south on Marconi Blvd., and started to pass Broad street. PO started to turn, but it was too late and PO stated she missed her turn. PO continued to go south and became lost. PO continued south until W Mound St., PO then went east and north on S Front St. PO was able to point to the direction of the clerk's, but continued north passing multiple streets to turn. FTO then had to assist PO in directions and driving to the clerk's. PO then went to the clerks and gathered case numbers for the fresh charge. PO started to go the correct direction to FCCS2 (Jackson Pike due to new changes in slating procedures for males). PO knew she needed to go on I71 south, but was unsure how to get on the freeway, and only saw I70 signs. FTO had to assist with getting PO to I71 south. PO arrived and talked with jail personal for pre-screening. The arrestee refused to exit the cruiser. PO was able to use the correct amount of force and escort the prisoner to the slating desk. PO communicated with the desk and properly slated the prisoner. On the next day PO and FTO discussed PO's not being able to locate the Clerk's Office, FTO showed PO a map of downtown and explained that there are multiple ways to get to the place in downtown. PO and FTO also went over when and why officer shall process prisoners though the Identification Unit. FTO and PO also went over when officer can bypass going through the Identification Unit.

PO volunteered to respond on a call for assistance from a woman wanting to collect her children and personal possessions from a sibling who had taken out a protection order against her. PO used the cruiser map to find a direct route to the location, demonstrating proper driving skills in transit. PO positioned the cruiser a safe distance from the location, and made a safe approach to the caller, who was awaiting officers outside. PO used good communication skills to obtain the woman's identifiers and a statement. As the woman had no photo ID, PO verified the woman’s' identity via LEADS and the Columbus Police Mugshots Application. PO neglected to ensure the woman had a copy of the protection order so he could review the limitations of that document. FTO requested the document and reviewed it, reminding PO that there may be restrictions in place preventing the woman from going to the residence in question. PO found the order had not yet been entered into LEADS, but recognized that the order was in force since the caller had a copy in her possession. PO made a cautious approach to the residence and made contact with the complainant in the order, advising her of the reason for officers' presence. PO used good communication skills to mediate the transfer of children and property. After clearing, FTO directed PO to review the Patrol SOP for 17B calls to ensure that he had navigated the call correctly. PO found that he should complete a DV stat sheet for the call, since both parties were present, and that course of action is indicated. PO opened a correctly classified case folder and completed a DV worksheet in an acceptable time frame of approximately 3 minutes.

PO responded to the report of domestic violence along with another training unit that involved two brothers fighting. PO found the location without assistance and arrived just as the other officers made contact. The caller stated her brothers engaged in a shoving match over a phone cord but it was now over and one of the brothers left for the night. PO spoke with the caller to confirm there was no domestic violence and the problem was solved for the time being. PO checked all involved parties for warrants and cleared the scene. FTO reviewed with PO what form was necessary to complete the run. With assistance PO was able to determine that a domestic incident stat sheet was necessary and remembered where it is located. The other training unit completed the stat sheet due for training as PO had already completed several.

text: PO responded to the location on a crash report. PO found the location with little FTO assistance, parked and approached safely. section: FTO Traffic Crash Investigation; Example Narratives
text: PO was dispatched on a hit/skip traffic crash involving an injury. PO used the cruiser map and found a direct course to the location, demonstrating proper driving skills in transit. PO noted upon arrival that the victim had moved off the roadway, onto a parking lot. PO positioned the cruiser a safe distance from the vehicle, and made a safe approach. PO made an acceptable decision not to activate the cruiser beacons as the involved party was off the roadway. PO interviewed the driver of the victim vehicle, and verified that the crash had occurred on the roadway, and that the other involved party was not at scene. PO used good interview skills to obtain the victim driver's identifiers, and statement. PO obtained a description of the hit/skip vehicle, and provided that information to another officer circulating the area. PO learned that Medics had already responded and left without transporting the victim driver. After providing the victim driver with a report number and ensuring he had no further questions, PO relocated to meet the other officer who had found a possible vehicle involved. PO investigated and determined the located vehicle was not the suspect vehicle. PO moved to a safe location, where he completed an OH-1 Crash Report in the OLEIS application in an acceptable time frame of approximately 22 minutes

section: FTO Traffic Crash Investigation; Example Narratives
text: PO responded to a report of a hit-skip traffic crash, caller reports that the suspect vehicle left its license plate at scene. PO drove a direct route to the location, on arrival he positioned his cruiser properly so as to block the victim's vehicle from being struck by on-coming traffic. PO made contact with the driver and obtained all necessary information for his report. PO collected the license plate left behind by the suspect vehicle. Prior to officer’s arrival, the victim had already contacted a wrecker to respond to scene. While waiting for the wrecker, FTO asked PO if he was responsible for investigating a hit-skip crash, PO stated he believed that officers were not responsible for this but opted to check the Patrol SOP & D.D. 5.05 "Traffic Crash Investigations" to be sure. PO found that he was responsible for completing the hit-skip investigation. Another officer at scene offered to assist PO. PO asked if he would be willing to drive to the registered address from the at-fault vehicle and attempt to make contact with its owner, if applicable. While waiting for the other officer to complete follow-up, PO remained at scene and began entering his information to complete the OH-1 report. PO was advised that the at-fault vehicle had not yet returned to its registered address. FTO/PO cleared from the crash scene once the tow truck cleared. Because the at-fault vehicle registered to an address nearby, PO decided to check it once more for the vehicle. PO located the address via Google maps and began driving to it. At this time a shot-spotter alert indicated shots fired very close to where FTO/PO currently were. PO pulled off his follow-up investigation and responded to the shots fired call. As officers completed the arrest for the shot-spotter run, PO continued working on his accident report. By this time, the end of shift had come and PO had not completed any investigation into the hit-skip other than having another officer check the registered address for the vehicle. The license plate left at scene by the at-fault vehicle was turned into the property room as evidence. PO completed the property slip and submission process with no assistance from FTO. PO later completed the crash report. Total completion time was approximately 90 minutes which was excessive; however, the report content was accurate. PO stated that he initially completed the report and realized that his diagram was not oriented correctly so he had to redo it. Additionally, upon proofreading his own narrative PO decided that he should re-write it so that it was better structured.

section: FTO Traffic Crash Investigation; Example Narratives
text: FTO advised PO to respond to a hit / skip accident report. PO collected the necessary information for the report without FTO assistance. PO is becoming more comfortable in interviewing people. PO started the crash report at 9:00pm and advised FTO he was complete except for one error he could not figure out at 10:45pm. FTO was able to assist PO in fixing the error that is tricky to fix, but required at least 28 other corrections throughout the report. Some of the errors such as the crash times, locations, cruiser district, and crash details. The diagram was not accurate at all and PO struggled to correct it without assistance. The narrative of the report overall depicted the crash but needed condensed. The report was complete at 12:40am. PO took an unacceptable amount of time to complete the report and struggled with accuracy. FTO again asked PO how she can help him improve his report writing skills because he continues to make the same mistakes. PO does not seem to understand when he spends time working on reports alone and he does not seem to learn from FTO going through corrections. FTO plans to focus on improving paperwork.

section: FTO Traffic Crash Investigation; Example Narratives
text: PO was dispatched to 176 E Norwich Ave on a disturbance where the caller believed they located a hit skip suspect vehicle. PO drove to the location and pulled in front of 125 E Norwich Ave and saw a vehicle matching the description provided in the run and parked the cruiser. PO approached the occupied vehicle and made contact with the driver who did not know anything about a crash. PO went to the rear of 125 E Norwich Ave believing he was in the correct location. PO then drove to 176 E Norwich St and spoke with the caller. PO gathered necessary information for a crash report. PO made contact with the owner of the suspect vehicle who advised the damage was old and pointed out evidence corroborating the claim. PO completed the traffic crash report in approximately one hour with very minimal FTO assistance. PO stated he was at the wrong location because he misread the map and then saw a vehicle matching the description provided on the run so he believed he was at the correct location. PO stated that his navigational error was not due to him misreading numbers but due to misreading a map and incorrectly assuming he was at the correct location when he saw the vehicle.

FTO Traffic Stop: Example Narrative

PO observed a vehicle turn without signaling from an improper lane and did an acceptable job of conducting a traffic stop. PO followed the vehicle into a gas station and activated the beacons. The vehicle stopped at a place that did not allow PO to properly position the cruiser. PO initially aired just the stop but before approaching added the license plate to the run and turned on the spotlight. PO failed to run the license plate in LEADS before approaching and later discussed slowing down. PO identified the driver and elected to release her with a warning. PO completed the traffic data collection without assistance.

PO and FTO were on patrol when PO observed a vehicle with an equipment violation. FTO pulled out behind the vehicle and paced the unit that was also exceeding the speed limit. PO properly aired the traffic stop and did a passenger side approach. PO made proper contact and retrieved identification from the driver. PO recognized the license provided was expired. PO properly checked the OL status and checked for warrants. PO decided to issue a citation for the moving violation. PO had a difficult time finding the correct code for the violation and required FTO assistance. PO completed the traffic citation in 14 minutes. PO properly issued the citation and ended the stop. Following the termination of the stop, PO properly completed the Traffic Data Collection. Following the stop, FTO spoke with PO about reducing the completion time on his traffic cites and told PO he needed to become more familiar with the traffic codes. PO stated he understood.

PO and FTO were on patrol when PO initiated a traffic stop at the listed location. PO made contact with the driver and was following the appropriate procedures. When PO asked for the driver's license, the driver stated he did not have his card on him. PO seemed confused, and FTO asked the clarifying questions to determine if it was just the physical ID or if the driver did not have a valid license. The driver responded informing PO he did not have his physical card on him. PO then immediate began to extract the driver from the vehicle and started to handcuff him. FTO went around the cruiser and inquired about the action. PO stated he was detaining the driver and placing him in handcuffs for not having his Driver's License on his person. FTO stopped the action and directed PO on how to proceed. PO then properly obtained identifying information to conduct the necessary checks on the driver. During the checks, PO discovered the driver did not possess a valid operator's license. PO recognized he now had grounds to remove the driver and affect an arrest. However, when PO made contact with the driver, he failed to inform him of the arrest and used poor prisoner control when extracting the driver. PO completed the traffic citation in an unacceptable amount of time (15 minutes), but with no errors or FTO assistance. PO then responded to the substation to complete the arrest paperwork. The u-10.100 was completed in 42 minutes with some minor errors. PO then went to the clerk's to retrieve the active warrants and get a case number for the fresh charges. Following such, PO transported the arrestee to FCJ to be slated. PO followed all of the appropriate procedures for the slating. The arrestee was medically refused at FCJ. With FTO prompting, PO properly aired the information. FTO then explained to PO they would go back to the Clerk's Office to try to obtain a court date for the warrants and change the fresh charges to a summons. FTO made contact with the assigned judge on the warrants and was able to have them set aside. PO then issued the arrestee the summons for the fresh charges and transported the subject to Grant Hospital. PO followed all of the appropriate procedures for such. PO was then unsure of what the required actions were. FTO instructed PO to reference his books for guidance. PO discovered he needed to complete a separate Hospital Transport Report. PO completed the P1 report and the Hospital Transport Report in 72 minutes. Following the completion, FTO spoke with PO about the requirement for him to have working knowledge of case law and his legal boundaries. PO was directed to review Arrest, Search, and Seizure sections relevant to traffic stops. FTO informed PO he also needed to work on his multi-tasking to be more efficient during the stop once he made the arrest. Due to the poor vehicle extraction, FTO walked PO through a vehicle extraction, conducted a practical demonstration, and demonstrated how FTO conducts vehicle extractions. PO stated he understood his unacceptable actions during the stop.

PO and FTO were on patrol when PO observed a moving violation and initiated a traffic stop. During the stop, PO followed all of the appropriate procedures and conducted himself in a safe manner. PO decided to issue a warning and terminate the stop. Following the stop, PO completed the Traffic Data Collection Form, in an acceptable amount of time, and with no errors or FTO assistance. No deficiencies were observed during this call for service.

PO observed an equipment violation and initiated a traffic stop. PO made contact, but failed to properly clear the backseat and process a juvenile that was in the car without a car seat. PO obtained the necessary information from the driver, but was completely unaware of the juvenile moving around in the backseat with the other backseat occupant trying to hide the child. PO decided to issue a citation and completed such in an acceptable amount of time. PO issued the citation for the equipment violation, but, again, failed to process the juvenile in the back. The car left the stop location. FTO asked PO how many occupants were in the vehicle. It took PO several minutes to give FTO his final answer. PO's response showed FTO that PO clearly was not paying attention to the occupants in the vehicle. FTO explained to PO this was not acceptable. PO was reminded he has an obligation to clear the backseat and process it before moving forward in the vehicle. FTO further reiterated the officer safety issue with his lack of processing. PO stated he understood.

PO was on patrol and ran a license plate that returned with the owner having a suspended license. PO stated he could not see the driver to know if they matched the physical description of the owner. The vehicle pulled into a gas station and up to a pump. PO circled the vehicle and saw the driver matched the physical description. PO aired the traffic stop. However, PO used none of his EVO equipment to alert the vehicle to the stop. PO also looked at FTO and stated he had a consensual encounter. The driver of the vehicle began to exit. PO failed to give any orders to keep the driver inside. PO then allowed the driver to remain by the opened door instead of bringing her back away from the unknown. PO questioned the drive while she was in the unsafe area and confirmed she was the listed person with the suspended license. PO then took the driver into custody, but failed to inform her she was under arrest. PO needed some help with his multi-tasking during the stop. PO completed the traffic cite in an acceptable amount of time, with no FTO assistance. PO completed the P1 report, with some errors and needing FTO guidance to the FRM. Following the run, FTO questioned PO as to why he didn't use any of his equipment to alert the driver of the stop. FTO further asked about the officer safety issue with letting the driver exit the vehicle and then allowing them to stay right by the door. PO had no excuse as to why he allowed this to happen. PO stated he didn't know why he said he had a consensual encounter immediately after airing his traffic stop. FTO informed PO the lapses of judgment had to stop and the officer safety issues were not acceptable. PO stated he understood.

While on patrol, PO noticed a vehicle that failed to use the turn signal. PO initiated a traffic stop, marking with radio her correct location and tag information. PO made a safe approach, the driver stated he was valid but left it at home. PO gathered the driver's information and attempted to locate him in LEADs. PO then gathered further information that the driver was visiting from Colorado, and only had a Colorado License. PO ran the driver through LEADs and located the driver. PO decided to issue a warning. PO made a safe approach and properly closed. PO then completed a Traffic Data Collection Form and classified the CVS. PO cleared via radio.

PO observed an equipment violation on a vehicle. PO ran the vehicle through LEADS, then aired his location prior to making a traffic stop. PO activated the lights and siren as the vehicle was stopped at the stop sign on S Richardson Ave at Wicklow Rd. Because of where PO initiated the traffic stop, the vehicle pulled just past the intersection and stopped, forcing PO to stop the cruiser in the middle of the intersection. PO found the driver was suspended and placed him under arrest. During an impound inventory of the vehicle, PO located a loaded firearm in a book bag on the passenger seat. PO requested additional unit respond to take pictures then completed a search of the vehicle locating a softball size baggie of marijuana. PO contacted a gun crimes detective. PO/FTO transported arrestee through CPD HQ ID then 5th floor to be interviewed. PO completed appropriate report with help from the FTO. PO/FTO then slated arrestee in Franklin County Jail. PO/FTO transported the firearm and marijuana and submitted it to the property room.
